articleBody:
DÜSSELDORF. **Künstliche Intelligenz gehört längst zum Berufsalltag vieler Lehrkräfte. Viele erleben die Technologie als Arbeitserleichterung. Doch mit ihrer Verbreitung wächst offenbar auch der Druck: Mehr als 40 Prozent der in Nordrhein-Westfalen befragten Lehrkräfte befürchten berufliche Nachteile, wenn sie auf KI verzichten, zahlreiche rechnen mit steigenden Anforderungen an ihre Arbeit. Gleichzeitig fehlen an den meisten Schulen verbindliche Regeln für den Umgang mit der Technologie. Das zeigt eine neue Umfrage des Philologenverbands Nordrhein-Westfalen (PhV NRW) – und wirft die Frage auf, ob aus einem freiwilligen Hilfsmittel zunehmend eine berufliche Erwartung wird.**

Guten Morgen, Herr Schröder. (Symbolbild) Illustration: Shutterstock

Die Nutzung künstlicher Intelligenz hat sich unter Lehrkräften innerhalb weniger Jahre erheblich verbreitet. Unterrichtsstunden vorbereiten, Arbeitsmaterialien erstellen, Aufgaben entwickeln oder Informationen recherchieren: Für solche Tätigkeiten greifen viele Pädagoginnen und Pädagogen inzwischen regelmäßig auf KI-Systeme zurück. Was vor wenigen Jahren noch eine technische Neuerung war, ist für einen großen Teil der Kollegien zum Arbeitsmittel geworden.

## KI ist im Lehreralltag angekommen – die Angebote des Landes spielen kaum eine Rolle

Wie weit diese Entwicklung fortgeschritten ist, zeigt die vierte Umfrage des Philologenverbands Nordrhein-Westfalen zum Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz in Schule und Unterricht. An der Befragung vom 4. bis 27. September 2026 beteiligten sich 1.205 Lehrkräfte, überwiegend von Gymnasien und Gesamtschulen. Rund 31 Prozent geben an, KI-Systeme mehrmals wöchentlich für ihre Arbeit einzusetzen, weitere 14 Prozent sogar täglich. 29 Prozent nutzen sie gelegentlich, 18 Prozent eher selten. Lediglich rund neun Prozent verzichten vollständig darauf – bei der ersten Befragung des Verbands im Jahr 2023 hatten noch 54 Prozent der Teilnehmenden angegeben, keine KI zu verwenden.

„Viele unserer Kolleginnen und Kollegen erkennen nach anfänglichen Vorbehalten mittlerweile einen echten Nutzen in den Chatbots“, erklärt die PhV-Landesvorsitzende Sabine Mistler. „Mit dem Nutzen steigt auch die Akzeptanz.“

Tatsächlich geben 55,6 Prozent der Befragten an, dass KI-Systeme ihre tägliche Arbeit sehr oder zumindest etwas erleichtern. Besonders Lehrkräfte mit geringer Berufserfahrung bewerten die Entlastung häufiger als groß. Sie setzen die Systeme auch intensiver ein: Während jüngere Kolleginnen und Kollegen häufiger täglich oder mehrmals wöchentlich mit KI arbeiten, überwiegt bei länger unterrichtenden Lehrkräften die gelegentliche Nutzung.

Dabei dominieren kommerzielle Anwendungen. Unter den hauptsächlich genutzten Systemen liegt ChatGPT mit 66,8 Prozent deutlich vorn. Es folgen Gemini mit 31,1 Prozent und die Anwendungen von Fobizz mit 30,2 Prozent.

Die vom Land Nordrhein-Westfalen bereitgestellten KI-Assistenten spielen dagegen bislang kaum eine Rolle. Seit Anfang Juni 2026 stellt das Land Lehrkräften vier entsprechende Anwendungen zur Verfügung, die unter anderem bei der Unterrichtsplanung, der Gestaltung von Lernsituationen und der Entwicklung von Medienkonzepten unterstützen sollen. Doch lediglich 4,8 Prozent der Befragten nutzen diese Angebote. 56,4 Prozent verwenden sie nicht, weitere 38,8 Prozent kennen sie überhaupt nicht.

## Aus Arbeitserleichterung könnte zusätzlicher Leistungsdruck werden

Die breite Nutzung künstlicher Intelligenz geht allerdings mit erheblichen Sorgen einher. Viele Lehrkräfte befürchten, ohne die Technologie beruflich nicht mehr mithalten zu können. 41,8 Prozent der Befragten befürchten, dass ihnen künftig berufliche Nachteile entstehen könnten, wenn sie auf KI verzichten. 39,5 Prozent teilen diese Sorge nicht, 18,7 Prozent sind unsicher. Damit sieht sich ein erheblicher Teil der Lehrkräfte mit einem zumindest empfundenen Erwartungsdruck konfrontiert.

Zugleich rechnen 39,3 Prozent damit, dass durch KI die Anforderungen an Umfang oder Qualität ihrer Arbeit steigen. 30,4 Prozent nennen Arbeitsverdichtung als eine ihrer größten Sorgen beim Einsatz der Technologie. Dahinter steht die Befürchtung, dass die durch KI eingesparte Arbeitszeit nicht zu einer tatsächlichen Entlastung führt, sondern zusätzliche Aufgaben und höhere Leistungserwartungen nach sich zieht.

## KI stellt die Leistungsbewertung infrage – Lehrkräfte suchen nach neuen Prüfungsformen

Die Herausforderung besteht allerdings nicht nur darin, mit den technischen Entwicklungen Schritt zu halten. Lehrkräfte müssen zugleich entscheiden, wie künstliche Intelligenz im Unterricht eingesetzt werden kann und wie sich unter diesen Bedingungen die Leistungen von Schülerinnen und Schülern noch zuverlässig bewerten lassen.

Gerade die Leistungsbewertung bereitet vielen erhebliche Schwierigkeiten. Rund 41 Prozent der Befragten erklären, künstliche Intelligenz habe die bisherige Bewertung schulischer Leistungen eher stark oder sehr stark verändert. Schon in der Umfrage des Vorjahres hatten 93 Prozent intransparente Eigenleistungen von Schülerinnen und Schülern als Herausforderung beim KI-Einsatz im Unterricht genannt.

„Die Notengebung ist durch KI komplexer geworden“, sagt Mistler.

Wie sich diese Veränderung im Unterricht bemerkbar machen kann, schildert eine Lehrkraft in den Freitextantworten der aktuellen Befragung: „Es fällt auf, dass die mündlichen Beiträge im Unterricht qualitativ zunehmend stark von den schriftlichen Leistungen (Klausuren, Tests, andere Angaben) abweichen. Daraus ergibt sich ein teils widersprüchliches und diffuses Leistungsbild der Schüler.“ Die Lehrkraft führt diese Beobachtung auf die Nutzung von KI im laufenden Unterricht zurück.

In den Freitextantworten sprechen sich zahlreiche Befragte deshalb für eine stärkere Gewichtung mündlicher Prüfungen, handschriftlicher Arbeiten und unter Aufsicht erbrachter Leistungen aus. Vorgeschlagen werden zusätzliche Prüfungsgespräche, Kolloquien und Aufgabenformate, bei denen sich fachliche Kenntnisse unmittelbar überprüfen lassen.

Auch etablierte Prüfungsformen geraten dadurch unter Druck. Einzelne Lehrkräfte stellen Facharbeiten infrage, weil sich bei zu Hause erstellten Texten nicht zuverlässig nachvollziehen lasse, in welchem Umfang sie selbstständig entstanden seien. Ähnliche Bedenken richten sich gegen die geplante Präsentationsprüfung im fünften Abiturfach. Andere Befragte fordern technische Möglichkeiten zur Erkennung oder Verhinderung des KI-Einsatzes, vereinzelt sogar Störsender in Klassenräumen.

Die Vorstellungen darüber, wie Schulen auf diese Entwicklung reagieren sollten, gehen allerdings auseinander. Während manche Lehrkräfte den Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz bei Prüfungen möglichst verhindern möchten, plädieren andere dafür, die Technologie in den Unterricht zu integrieren und zugleich neue Formen der Leistungsbewertung zu entwickeln.

Eine Lehrkraft formuliert diesen Anspruch in den Freitextantworten so: „Wir werden nicht mehr drumherum kommen, KI in unsere Arbeit und die Arbeit der SuS‘ zu integrieren, müssen es jedoch schaffen, das Erbringen von authentischen Eigenleistungen weiterhin im Sinne der Erziehung unserer SuS‘ zu mündigen BürgerInnen unserer Gesellschaft zu ermöglichen (denn das sehe ich nach wie vor als einen unserer wichtigsten Aufträge).“

Neben der Leistungsbewertung bereitet den Befragten auch die Zuverlässigkeit der Systeme Sorgen. 70,1 Prozent nennen fehlerhafte Ergebnisse als eine der größten Herausforderungen. 42,9 Prozent verweisen auf Datenschutzprobleme. 41,7 Prozent befürchten, dass durch die Auslagerung geistiger Tätigkeiten an KI eigene kognitive Fähigkeiten verloren gehen könnten.

Die Sorge richtet sich damit nicht nur auf technische Fehler, sondern auch auf mögliche Folgen für das Lernen und Denken. Mehr als 70 Prozent der Befragten sehen Handlungsbedarf bei der wissenschaftlichen Abschätzung der Auswirkungen künstlicher Intelligenz auf Kinder und Jugendliche.

Dabei gibt es durchaus Stimmen, die vor einer einseitigen Problemdebatte warnen. Eine Lehrkraft schreibt in den Freitextantworten: „Zu viel Blick auf Sorgen, zu wenig Blick auf konstruktiven Umgang und die Chancen; Gerade befinden wir uns gesellschaftlich in einer Umbruchphase, in der sich noch herausstellen wird, was möglich und praktikabel sein wird. Die Potenziale sind enorm im Bereich der Arbeitserleichterung.“

## An den meisten Schulen fehlen verbindliche Regeln für den KI-Einsatz

Die unterschiedlichen Einschätzungen verdeutlichen, wie sehr sich die Schulen noch in einer Phase der Orientierung befinden. Während die Technologie längst im Alltag angekommen ist, fehlen vielerorts verbindliche Regeln für ihren Einsatz. Nur 28,3 Prozent der Befragten geben an, dass es an ihrer Schule Vorgaben zur KI-Nutzung gibt. 57,4 Prozent erklären, entsprechende Regelungen existierten nicht. Weitere 14,3 Prozent wissen nicht, ob solche Vorgaben vorhanden sind.

Zwar hat sich der Anteil der Schulen mit bekannten KI-Regelungen seit 2023 mehr als verdoppelt. Damals hatten lediglich 13 Prozent der Befragten entsprechende Vorgaben bestätigt. Dennoch arbeitet die Mehrheit der Lehrkräfte nach eigener Auskunft weiterhin ohne verbindliche schulinterne Orientierung. „Der überwiegende Teil der Lehrkräfte arbeitet nach wie vor ohne bekannte Regeln“, stellt Mistler fest. „Dabei steht der Wunsch nach Vorgaben zur rechtskonformen Nutzung seit unserer ersten Befragung weit oben auf dem Wunschzettel der Kolleginnen und Kollegen.“

Auch staatliche Unterstützungsangebote erreichen viele Lehrkräfte bislang nicht. Bereits bei der Befragung im Vorjahr hatten 49 Prozent der Teilnehmenden angegeben, den KI-Handlungsleitfaden des nordrhein-westfälischen Schulministeriums nicht zu kennen. Die geringe Bekanntheit der inzwischen bereitgestellten landeseigenen KI-Assistenten fügt sich in dieses Bild.

## Philologenverband fordert mehr Zeit und Ressourcen für den Umgang mit KI

Der Philologenverband fordert vor diesem Hintergrund mehr Unterstützung für die Kollegien. Die Einführung künstlicher Intelligenz dürfe nicht dazu führen, dass steigende Anforderungen an die Arbeit der Lehrkräfte als selbstverständlich vorausgesetzt würden.

„Dass künstliche Intelligenz gleichzeitig Chance und Herausforderung ist, zeigt unsere mittlerweile vierte Umfrage noch einmal deutlich“, erklärt Mistler. „Auf der einen Seite erleichtert sie unseren Kolleginnen und Kollegen an manchen Stellen die tägliche Arbeit, auf der anderen Seite sehen wir die Gefahr, dass dadurch die Ansprüche des Dienstherrn, was Arbeitsumfang und -qualität angeht, steigen. Viele Lehrkräfte fühlen sich unter Druck gesetzt, mit Chatbots arbeiten zu müssen. Gerade in größeren Schulsystemen wie Gymnasien und Gesamtschulen brauchen wir deshalb mehr Ressourcen und Zeit, um den Umgang mit KI zu professionalisieren und der rasanten Entwicklung standhalten zu können.“ *News4teachers*

articleBody:
Stepping back from the specifics of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) debate, I want to make a larger point about the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and its role in American public policy:

This law has “environmental” in its title, but in a critical respect it’s just not an environmental law at all.

Which is to say it does not set any kind of standards related to environmental quality. The Clean Air Act makes rules about air pollution. The Clean Water Act makes rules about water pollution. We could make stricter rules about microplastics or forever chemicals or something else. We also have parks and other kinds of wildlife and landscape conservation programs.

None of this is NEPA.

NEPA is a law that makes it harder to do certain classes of things by imposing various procedural requirements, and it creates a litigation attack surface for people who do not like these classes of things.

NEPA is entirely indifferent as to whether the proposed thing is good for the environment or bad for the environment. What’s more, unlike real environmental laws, NEPA does not govern private-sector economic activity. The key idea of NEPA is the “major federal action.” It burdens government activities relative to private-sector activities and it burdens “action” (doing something new) relative to the status quo.

If you want to cut taxes on business investment to encourage more data center construction, that’s not a federal action for NEPA purposes, even though common sense says that tax law is a very important facet of federal policy. Maintaining the regulatory status quo is not a federal action even if the status quo is bad for the environment. If you want to build a light rail line that’s partially financed with a Department of Transportation grant, that’s a federal action and you need to do your NEPA homework.

If requiring federal (but not private) actions (but not inactions) to meet a set of burdensome procedural requirements leads to better environmental outcomes than not doing this, that would have to be essentially by coincidence.

I think a lot of progressive analytical errors about the post-1970 history of the United States are downstream of not understanding this.

It’s not just that progressives overrate NEPA but that they have an essentially false narrative of why contemporary government is the way it is. There’s this view that something called “neoliberalism” happened and that now because of “neoliberalism,” all the Democrats do is hand out tax credits rather than being cool New Dealers who support a robust state. But guess what — a tax credit to buy electric cars is not a major federal action but a mass transit line is.

NEPA is not the only reason for the rise of what [Suzanne Mettler calls the “submerged state”](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0226521656?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback) or what [Mike Konczal calls government by coupon](https://www.newamerica.org/insights/no-discount-comparing-the-public-option-to-the-coupon-welfare-state/), but it’s striking that progressives tend to neglect its existence while workaday bureaucrats are painfully aware of its relevance.

#### The bias toward inaction

When New York City was thinking about launching its congestion pricing program to reduce traffic in parts of Manhattan and raise revenue for mass transit, it was granted the grace of being allowed to comply with NEPA via an environmental assessment rather than the more burdensome environmental impact statement. That less burdensome document runs [868 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93446) with a two-volume appendix. The first volume of the appendix has [1,966 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93451) and the [second volume is 1,173 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93456). Yes, that is 4,000 pages worth of environmental review under the *less* burdensome of the two NEPA tracks for a program that charges people money to drive cars and uses the revenue to fund mass transit.

The reason the report has to be so long is not because the question of whether this is bad for the environment is hard to answer.

articleBody:
Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt. Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann.

**Elisabeth Waczek** ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des [Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)](https://www.prif.org/forschung/cntr), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit.

**Seit dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine wird deutlich intensiver über Sicherheit und militärische Technologien diskutiert. Spüren Sie seit der Gründung Ihres Forschungsclusters 2023 ein wachsendes Interesse an Ihrer Arbeit?**

Wir spüren definitiv ein wachsendes Interesse.

Unser Fokus liegt auf Rüstungskontrolle im weiteren Sinne. Wir beschäftigen uns mit der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit. Zu Beginn habe ich es als eine deutlich größere Herausforderung wahrgenommen, die Relevanz dessen zu erklären. Mittlerweile merke ich: Das haben viele Leute auf dem Schirm. Diese Themen sind stark ins Bewusstsein gerückt. Viele Leute in Europa haben nun das Gefühl, wir müssen uns wieder stärker mit dem Thema Sicherheit auseinandersetzen.

**Ihr Forschungscluster beschäftigt sich mit Technologien, die bestehende Machtverhältnisse verändern könnten. Woran erkennen Sie, dass eine technologische Entwicklung über die Fachcommunity hinaus sicherheitspolitisch relevant wird?**

Unsere Mitarbeitenden aus den Sozialwissenschaften und aus den Natur- und Technikwissenschaften kommen gemeinsam zu einer Einschätzung: Ist das eine Entwicklung, die disruptives Potenzial hat?

Konkret bedeutet das zum Beispiel: Lassen sich neue Technologien oder Forschungsergebnisse missbrauchen, um Waffen herzustellen? Welche Akteur*innen könnten Zugang bekommen, die ihn zuvor nicht hatten? Reicht bestehende Regulierung noch aus, um schädliche – vielleicht auch unbeabsichtigte – Folgen zu minimieren? Gefährlich wird es zum Beispiel, wenn Technologie die Dynamiken so stark beschleunigt, dass deeskalierende Instrumente wie die Rüstungskontrolle nicht mehr Schritt halten können, oder wenn sich nicht mehr feststellen lässt, woher eine Bedrohung kommt.

Interessanterweise kommen unsere Wissenschaftler*innen auch immer wieder zu der Einschätzung, dass dieses disruptive Potenzial gar nicht so dramatisch ist. Oft geht dem viel Hype voraus und besonders reißerische, aber vielleicht eher unwahrscheinliche Szenarien bekommen viel Aufmerksamkeit. Beim Thema KI zum Beispiel. Da ist es Aufgabe der Wissenschaft, erst einmal einen nüchterneren Blick einzunehmen und zu schauen: Wie gefährlich ist das denn wirklich? Welche Anwendungen haben das größte Potenzial negativer Auswirkungen und wo liegen womöglich auch Chancen? Am Ende kommt oft so etwas dabei raus wie: Ja, man muss das Thema ernst nehmen, aber man sollte nicht in Panik verfallen.

**Wenn Sie sich etwas für die gesellschaftliche Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung wünschen könnten: Was sollte die Öffentlichkeit aus Ihrer Sicht besser verstehen, um einen informierten Umgang mit diesen Themen zu ermöglichen?**

### Cluster Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)

Das CNTR am PRIF untersucht, wie neue Technologien und wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen die internationale Sicherheit beeinflussen. Forschende aus verschiedenen Disziplinen analysieren mögliche Risiken und Chancen technologischer Innovationen und entwickeln Empfehlungen, um die internationale Rüstungskontrolle zu stärken.

Ein Beispiel: Ich war auf einer Tagung, bei der die Sprache auf das Thema Dual-Use-Forschung kam. Das sind Forschung oder Technologien, die legitime zivile Anwendungen haben, aber auch in militärischer Weise gebraucht oder in illegitimer Weise missbraucht werden können.

Auf dieser Tagung hat jemand gesagt: „Ist doch ganz klar, Dual-Use-Forschung sollten wir einfach nicht machen.“ Das ist ein häufiges Missverständnis. Mittlerweile haben so viele Forschungsbereiche einen Dual-Use-Charakter, etwa große Teile der Informatik oder Medizin. In der Kommunikation tragen wir die Verantwortung, zu sagen: Nur weil eine Forschung Sicherheitsrisiken in sich trägt, ist diese Forschung nicht automatisch schlecht oder illegitim. Sie kann trotzdem wichtig sein.

Auch bei der Diskussion um Zivilklauseln, die in den letzten Jahren ziemlich intensiv geführt wurde, ist es wichtig, sich vor Augen zu führen, welche Funktion solche Instrumente überhaupt haben. Natürlich ist die Wissenschaftsfreiheit im Grundgesetz verankert. Genauso ist im Grundgesetz verankert, dass man als Forschende*r nicht einfach Massenvernichtungswaffen entwickeln kann. Interessant sind vor allem die Graubereiche, in denen Forschende viel Eigenverantwortung tragen müssen.

Es ist wichtig, dass Forschende mit dieser Verantwortung durch institutionelle Strukturen unterstützt werden. In der Wissenschaftskommunikation tragen wir dazu bei, das Bewusstsein für diese Themen zu schärfen.

**Wie gelingt es, im Diskurs um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung berechtigte Sorgen zu adressieren, ohne zu dramatisieren oder zu verharmlosen?**

Es ist wichtig zu beobachten, mit welchen Vokabeln und Bildsprache der Diskurs stattfindet, und das immer wieder kritisch zu reflektieren. Wir versuchen generell, Darstellungen, die als kriegs- oder gewaltbejahend empfunden werden können, zu vermeiden, ebenso martialische Bildsprache.

Wenn man Kommunikation als Handwerk lernt, bekommt man bestimmte Best Practices mit: wie Menschen Informationen aufnehmen und wie man Gehör findet. Dazu gehören Mittel wie: klare Botschaften, starke Verben, einfache Sätze, die im Gedächtnis bleiben. Wir müssen uns im Wettbewerb um Aufmerksamkeit gegen eine Flut an Desinformationen durchsetzen und brauchen diese Techniken. Aber gleichzeitig entziehen sich wissenschaftliche Inhalte durch die gebotene Nuancierung oft diesen Best-Practice-Leitlinien.

Diese grundlegende Spannung, die man in der Wissenschaftskommunikation immer hat, verstärkt sich im Umfeld sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung noch einmal mehr.

### „Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente“

Elisabeth Waczek

**Ihr Forschungscluster vereint naturwissenschaftliche und sozialwissenschaftliche Perspektiven. Wie wirkt sich dieser interdisziplinäre Ansatz auf die Art und Weise, wie Sie Forschungsergebnisse kommunizieren, aus?**

Eine spannende Alltagsbeobachtung für die Wissenschaftskommunikation ist, dass Menschen verschiedene Disziplinen unterschiedlich wahrnehmen. Bei manchen Disziplinen erkennen sie die erforderliche Fachexpertise leichter, bei anderen haben sie das Gefühl, jede*r könne mitreden.

Die Philosophie fällt dem manchmal stärker zum Opfer, weil sie viele Begriffe und Konzepte verwendet, die jeder im Alltag verwendet und kennt. Deswegen gibt es bestimmte Berührungsängste vielleicht weniger als mit der Molekularbiologie oder der Quantenphysik. Politik- und Sozialwissenschaften liegen irgendwo dazwischen. Natürlich hängt das auch davon ab, welche Berührungspunkte man selbst mit den entsprechenden Disziplinen hat. Und wir können beobachten, dass sich das auch verändert. Zum Beispiel in der Corona-Pandemie, als Fachbegriffe aus der Virologie und Epidemiologie plötzlich Einzug in alltägliche Gespräche gehalten haben.

Verschiedene Disziplinen erfordern in der Kommunikation auch unterschiedliche Ansätze. Die sozialwissenschaftlichen Themen muss man manchmal stärker von der alltäglichen Betrachtung wegrücken. Es liegt eine besondere Herausforderung darin, nicht nur zu vermitteln, was die Ergebnisse der Forschung in diesen Bereichen sind, sondern auch zu verdeutlichen: Was können Wissenschaftler*innen zu diesem Thema sagen, was ich als eine Person, die einfach nur Nachrichten schaut, dazu nicht sagen kann? Es geht also auch darum, bei unserem Zielpublikum eine gewisse Scientific Literacy mit aufzubauen. Auf der anderen Seite kann es im naturwissenschaftlichen Bereich wichtiger sein, die Themen näher an die Leute heranzurücken und vom Fachjargon in etwas zu übersetzen, woran sie anknüpfen können.

[Sicherheit & Innovation Alle Beiträge zum Jahresfokus](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/schwerpunkt-sicherheit-innovation/)

Die Interdisziplinarität erfordert dann, diese Ansätze zusammenzubringen. Wir reden gerade ganz allgemein von Wissenschaftskommunikation, aber wir haben natürlich unterschiedliche Zielgruppen, und die haben unterschiedliche Kenntnisstände. Es ist wichtig, sich das bewusst zu machen und eine Art modularen Ansatz zu wählen. Wir überlegen: Was sind die wichtigsten Kernbotschaften? Welche Hintergrundinformationen könnte eine Person brauchen, die nicht im Thema drin ist? Wie können wir visuelle Elemente einsetzen, um die Zugänglichkeit der Themen zu erhöhen?

**Wissenschaft sollte möglichst offen und transparent sein. Wenn es um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung geht, kann Transparenz jedoch auch Risiken bergen. Wo verläuft da die Grenze zwischen Offenheit und verantwortungsvollem Schutz?**

Das ist immer eine Abwägung im Einzelfall. Ich denke, die eigentliche, schwierigere Frage findet nicht erst in der Kommunikation statt, sondern schon früher. Bei einem großen Risikopotenzial ist die Frage grundlegend: Was kann ich davon überhaupt veröffentlichen?

Eine mögliche Maßnahme ist, nur einen Teil der Forschungsergebnisse in einem Journal zu veröffentlichen. Das beißt sich natürlich damit, wie Wissenschaft überhaupt funktioniert. Sie ist eigentlich auf Reproduzierbarkeit, Offenheit und Dialog angelegt. Die Wissenschaftskommunikation kann sich hier nicht gänzlich aus der Affäre ziehen. Allerdings denke ich, dass wir nicht diejenigen sind, die solche Abwägungen treffen können, weil sie selbst Gegenstand einer wissenschaftlichen Einschätzung sind.

Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente. Denn dadurch, dass man sagt: „Achtung, diese Forschung ließe sich missbrauchen auf diese und jene Art und Weise“, erzeugt man auch die Gefahr, dass man die Aufmerksamkeit auf das Missbrauchspotenzial lenkt. Auch wir Kommunikator*innen, die Aufmerksamkeit lenken wollen, müssen also umsichtig vorgehen.

articleBody:
This year brought a remarkably strong showing in fiction. Here is my list in the order I read them:

Siri Hustvedt, [Ghost Stories: A Memoir](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/05/what-ive-been-reading-288.html).

Karl Knausgaard, [The School of Night](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/02/the-school-of-night.html).

Juan Marsé, [Last Evenings with Teresa](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/05/last-evenings-with-teresa.html) [new translation]

Claudia Piñeiro, [Cathedrals](https://www.amazon.com/Cathedrals-Claudia-Pi%C3%B1eiro/dp/1917260288/ref=sr_1_1?crid=SG52MP17QWCV&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.Hu-QferChYhDEPWp5HEYnHhrFzkx1dg1gUSekcFZsro1oZzg1ryq87dqOgZkPMWcUysp8B6aoGzGsyyc7BY8SCWkEyn3L14hh3q0eqwqnyJ2RNKAxn_R2flh1wmFsku1m_h38bT6QLMxqp9eCbqhP4NV9OD1uBGOibG1Kbh4EF3KA3KruRN9gTJZv5VsFzG8Ig8Fbap1Q_b21bVqJJ5JM-fQGBt2rN0txwAcjaeVJOwP6ksoiIRenerbIxSrOknXHz3_Je4wSwsxNPuk_cH5B81RiV5jZKrd0FM05DFuF3A.F9aG1-_uCZlGaPG9-uQVU9ySChBiv4hY1paKHMRt49Y&dib_tag=se&keywords=Claudia+Pi%C3%B1eiro&qid=1795349645&sprefix=claudia+pi%C3%B1eiro%2Caps%2C683&sr=8-1).

Christian Kracht, [Eurotrash](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/07/what-ive-been-reading-292.html) [2025], and Air [2026].

Munir Hachemi, [The Mulai](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/08/what-ive-been-reading-294.html).

Olga Grjasnowa, [My Dreadful Body](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/my-dreadful-body.html).

China Mieville, [The Rouse](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/what-ive-been-reading-296.html) (still reading this one).

Ingeborg Bachmann and Max Frisch, [‘We Didn’t Do Very Well’: The Correspondence](https://www.amazon.com/We-Didnt-Very-Well-Correspondence/dp/1803096640/ref=sr_1_1?crid=XS5FHNB0PI8L&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.eqgX0lK3bTgrPTaeuy-lHqPCOwthPb_UHXvsLJ-u8MIXWyCVFgOw4NKRiOLmif3HeuWJyYRCatUwthBfnkhf93nsC5yquWQuh5djZk-SqXw3p7j380-4WUJxVZsWiDAmVxtFFiXn8DqGGdKuKz08pkT5zEr-q-S1EHjRRNUppEGdfjCdut43pEZ5kTFmy48k66qC04pfFVYS_S0jiffxwWlBAcHUrEXOerUHYRsAHwo.JH4i51O7OOZioF1FViC67Gv7Bi29Sy3ibtv2Unf2dqg&dib_tag=se&keywords=Ingeborg+Bachmann+and+Max+Frisch&qid=1795349513&sprefix=ingeborg+bachmann+and+max+frisch%2Caps%2C505&sr=8-1). Here are [my remarks on the German-language edition](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/mein-ingeborg-bachmann-studium.html).

Adolo Bioy Casares, [Morel’s Invention](https://www.amazon.com/Morels-Invention-Adolfo-Bioy-Casares/dp/B0GGNLYS96/ref=sr_1_1?crid=2DYCM1TBC52BO&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.qIbqYA39c4XZt0O40n6iqErl6DZr1ty1EQT7RYcHJFNHL0y4pxggeMSYSenPjlxHPU2dwkvROS1889ve5ixbMTueWV3MdLC5QXm6HlLPj5ktXmk8QyJY7XafgxrvqBFxYVCvkk_gpqsIFR3if0KOZiup8Kmr4N9NFCOKbVNVMfGoe6SuhnMh8RNWSrVk0y16tX0faXqZhFRneD3oYBlqJ5I2N2BD6-dBFPyVS4eafGM.zSd2WQH7Z25bF7xJihxYy1-QXzue5uZCkNMiDBiPplA&dib_tag=se&keywords=morel%27s+invention+by+adolfo+bioy+casares&qid=1795349588&sprefix=morel%27s+inven%2Caps%2C140&sr=8-1), new translation by Margaret Jull Costa.

Missouri Williams, [The Vivisectors](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

Mathias Enard, [Perfecting the Shot](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

M. John Harrison, [The End of Everything](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

Solvej Ball, [On the Calculation of Volume V](https://www.amazon.com/Calculation-Book-V-Solvej-Balle/dp/081124038X/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3GT8MBEP5BPBF&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.UfEYs0frpqxRucGNMTpDFzlPTb07Zpz4C74h_R1aMG5jW36OklQQk14FuH0zfIKMj0J5S-j7f3BtdPafSZ8kJWQEKVbsDVeA8tKAOs9FvFJEf0pTMAWhStpgPJeWn1SB.bl4g8dgv0ovDERrS8A2nJhKll5OBzhghwmhsxMQebII&dib_tag=se&keywords=On+the+Calculation+of+Volume+V&qid=1795349472&sprefix=%2Caps%2C130&sr=8-1), noting you cannot start at the fifth volume for this series.

There is also a new Min Lee novel, and a new and short Jon Fosse novel, as possible contenders for this list. I have not yet read them. As for a “best of,” the Knausgaard and the Bachmann-Frisch correspondence stand out for me, Bioy Casares as well.

What else? I do believe we are entering an era where high quality fiction is more and more important. I am delighted to see that our writers and translators are responding accordingly.

title: Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
subtitle: From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures.
feedText: Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs, draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes. Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel, the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on…
articleBody:
From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist [Su Blackwell](https://sublackwell.co.uk/) carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled *Pathway of Crumbs*, draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of *Hansel and Gretel*, the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

“Break off my Branches” (2025), paper cut sculpture and wooden frame without glass, 115 x 16 x 85 centimeters

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.

*Pathway of Crumbs* is on view from November 25 to January 25 at [Long & Ryle](https://longandryle.com/) in London. Find more from Blackwell on [her website](https://sublackwell.co.uk/).

title: When A Farewell to Arms Was Censored For Foul Language
subtitle: The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated.
feedText: Scribner’s Magazine had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, A Farewell to Arms, when it began serializing it in May 1929. The semi-autobiographical novel followed the experiences of an American ambulance driver on the Italian Front in World War I. articleBody:
The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated. *Scribner’s Magazine* had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839), when it began serializing it in May 1929. The semi-autobiographical novel followed the experiences of an American ambulance driver on the Italian Front in World War I. For publication as a book, Maxwell Perkins, Hemingway’s editor at Charles Scribner’s Sons, managed to get the last three phrases restored, in sentences such as “I shot the son of a bitch with my rifle,” “they were loading the girls from the soldiers’ whorehouse into a truck,” and “Jesus Christ what I could do with two hundred and fifty dollars.” Hemingway and Perkins negotiated, the editor conceding “scrotum” instead of “balls,” but refusing “c—s r” as an alternative to “cocksucker” (which became, instead, “‘I killed that – of a sergeant’ ”). The author had to turn his other “four-letter words” into phrases like “Go something yourself.” Hemingway protested that “emasculation was a minor operation to perform on men, animals, and books, but its effect was great.” He was waging a fight for “full use of the language.” But he gave in.

Hemingway had won part of his fight. But predictably, “scrotum,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” “Jesus Christ” (as an exclamation), and the premarital love affair at the novel’s core were themselves too much for the Word Police, at least in some jurisdictions. In Boston—a city already known for its gusto in banning any work of literature or art deemed indecent by officials—Police Superintendent Michael Crowley announced that the June issue of *Scribner’s* was being barred from sale because of its “salacious” material, even before the book version restored some of the offensive words. Scribner’s jumped to Hemingway’s defense, issuing a press release defending him as “one of the finest and most highly regarded of the modern writers,” and promised that it would continue serializing [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)in coming issues. But Scribner’s also felt called upon to underscore the novel’s “distinctly moral” nature. “It is the story of a fine and faithful love, born, it is true, out of physical desire,” the release continued. “If white is to be contrasted with black, thereby emphasizing its whiteness, the picture cannot be all white.”

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths.[/pullquotes]

This defense sidestepped the fact that Hemingway himself, an admirer of Mark Twain, would have rejected any notion of a simplistic “black” and “white” moral in his novel as a shabby evasion serving outmoded and dishonest values. But the press release went forth, and Scribner’s investment paid off. [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)sold 31,000 copies in its first print run and helped make its author financially independent. As book industry executives expected, being “banned in Boston” probably boosted sales—even among Bostonians, who could cross the city line to buy copies elsewhere. One of the passages in *[A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)* rang as a clarion call for turning ideas about what was “obscene” on their heads. In it, an Italian soldier, reflecting on the staggering death toll of a recent offensive, remarks that the sacrifice cannot have been “in vain.” In response, Hemingway’s protagonist, the American Frederic Henry, muses on the power and deceit of words:

I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain…I had seen nothing sacred, and the things that were glorious had no glory and the sacrifices were like the stockyards of Chicago if nothing was done with the meat except to bury it…Abstract words such as glory, honor, courage, or hallow were obscene beside the concrete names of villages, the numbers of roads, the names of rivers, the numbers of regiments and the dates.

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths. One form of language lied. The other, if used to register authentic emotional experience, didn’t. “Fuck,” “shit,” and “cocksucker” expressed real feelings in real speech. “Glory,” “honor,” and “courage” deluded.

Yet the miniature Culture War that [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)unleashed was also fought out behind closed doors in the Manhattan offices of Charles Scribner’s Sons. After all, Scribner’s and other prestige presses were themselves Word Police, upholding nineteenth-century aesthetic and moral ideals that company elders brought to their self-appointed roles as gatekeepers of American taste and cultivation, all while selling books and magazines to make money. Perkins had already run this gauntlet more than once. His elders at the house had objected loudly in 1922 when another of his young stars, F. Scott Fitzgerald, wanted to title a short story collection [Tales of the Jazz Age](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780307476371). The word “jazz” was the problem: they felt, Perkins explained, “that the word whatever implication it actually has, will itself injure the book.” But the title stayed, and, as Fitzgerald correctly predicted, “it will be bought by *my own personal public*, that is, by the countless flappers and college kids who think I am a sort of oracle.” Many of those flappers and collegians knew that jazz’s “implications” included semen, orgasm, and sex.

Hemingway’s first novel, [The Sun Also Rises](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780743297332), had almost been rejected by Scribner’s in 1926, despite Perkins’s advocacy. That novel’s spare account of emotionally rootless young Americans in post-World War I Europe bewildered the house’s older editors, and Hemingway and Perkins fought hard to retain the word “bitch” to describe the heroine, Lady Brett Ashley. As another writer observed, old “Charles Scribner would no sooner allow profanity in one of his books than he would invite friends to use his parlor as a toilet room.” The company had agreed to publication with great reluctance, resigning itself to the inevitable Boston banning. But *The Sun Also Rises* sold quickly; by the time of Hemingway’s death in 1961, an estimated million copies had circulated. Writing of the 1920s, the critic Edmund Wilson mused on the novel’s impact: “The great watchword was ‘Have a drink’; and in the bars of New York and Paris the young people were getting to talk like Hemingway.” As John Updike reflected decades later, “an entire generation of American men learned to speak in the accents of [his] stoicism.”

articleBody:
Art by Thomas Cole via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cole_Thomas_The_Course_of_Empire_Destruction_1836.jpg)

Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist.

Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call [the New Right](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/understanding-americas-new-right). In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to [wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization”](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/new-rights-grand-strategy-after-trump).

At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. It merged with the [Covid antivax movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-alternate-reality-of-rfk-and) to become skeptical of modern medicine, public health, and life science in general. It partially merged with [the incel movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/dating-advice-for-men), telling young men that their sexual frustration was the fault of progressivism. It [veered even more strongly into antisemitism](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/jewish-americans-are-feeling-unsettled), probably feeling liberated to do so by rising antisemitism on the left in the wake of the Gaza war. And it added a strong component of [anti-Indian hatred](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-anti-american-right), seeing Indians as a uniquely vulnerable target among recent immigrant groups.

Anyway, it’s too early to say that this movement has *failed*. Yes, the Democrats won one midterm election, but Trump is still the President, and he has shown zero inclination to reverse course on any of his most New Right-aligned policies. He has made Stephen Miller, the ultimate anti-immigration crusader, his chief of staff, and [posted a picture](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/europe/trump-friend-greeting-putin-causes-alarm-europe-ukraine-rcna610373) of himself hugging Vladimir Putin with the caption “My Friend”. Meanwhile, the New Right still has a fairly robust online presence.

But it’s impossible to deny that the winds have shifted. The midterms made it clear that even if the New Right sticks around for the long term, it won’t have a monopoly on power. That will make it essentially impossible for it to follow through on its long-term agenda. Basically, the notion that wokeness and internal disputes would cause the Democrats to permanently collapse as a party has been falsified.

Already, some prominent figures are backing away from the New Right. Elon Musk, who once stood on a stage and declared himself “Dark MAGA”, now says he’s not even MAGA at all, and is instead a political moderate:

And the CEO of Palantir is calling himself a Democrat:

Meanwhile, Bo French, the Texas candidate who lost an election after complaining about Indian fans at a UT football game, has been [kicked out of his country club](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-texas-country-club-membership-01173063).

The New Right’s online activists and commentators are in a state of deep despair:

Others are tweeting ever more histrionic demands for a civil war that absolutely no one seems interested in actually fighting:

What enthusiasm still *does* exist on the New Right tends to be concentrated on the movement’s most extreme fringe, which focuses on getting attention by bashing Trump and MAGA and saying ridiculous, extremist stuff. For example, *[Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242)* [reports](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242) on the “Christ is King” conference, run by a guy named Joel Webbon:

> [F]or Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn’t gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women’s right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office…The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker…
> There are, in Webbon’s telling, few “guys” capable of leading this faction…He did put forward a few “guys” who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like [James] Fishback, one of the weekend’s main draws, who recently lost [a gubernatorial primary] to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida…Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

(There are also various [loonies from overseas](https://vimeo.com/1248089901?fl=pl&fe=vl).)

These are all signs of a movement that’s on the way down. It may return someday — communism sort of did, after all — but its hopes of transforming America over the next few decades are fading. It’s not over yet, but it’s looking more and more that way.

A big part of the reason for that failure, of course, is that Americans simply do not buy what the New Right wants to sell them. Regular Americans [generally like (legal) immigration](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712289/americans-support-immigration-down-strong.aspx), and they [don’t see racial and religious heritage](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/52636-what-makes-someone-american-heritage-constitution-declaration) as an important determinant of who is a real American. It’s very hard to sell people a product they don’t want.

But there are also various strategic errors that the New Right made. To be clear, I’m *glad* these mistakes were made; I have zero desire to see a movement like the New Right hold power in my country. I just think it’s interesting and instructive to think about what the mistakes were.

One choice that *wasn’t* a mistake was to hitch the movement to Donald Trump. A lot of people in the New Right are going to blame their failure on [Trump’s mistake](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-second-trump-presidency-is-a)s — his Iran War, his corruption, and his reluctance to do anything about inflation. But without the assistance from Trump’s personal charisma and idiosyncratic broad appeal, it’s doubtful that the New Right would ever have escaped the basement of the internet in the first place; the Republican establishment would have kept it locked in a box, the way they did with similar insurgencies from Pat Buchanan and the John Birch Society in past eras. Trump was actually the *most effective* leader the New Right could have chosen.

Instead, the New Right’s weakness mostly sprang from the fact that it was an online movement.

#### Reactionary impatience

Rightists will tell you that American culture has been completely captured by the left. And when you ask how this was accomplished, they’ll tell you about the “long march through the institutions” — a strategy that [a German leftist described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_march_through_the_institutions) in the 1960s. Basically, the idea was for leftists to infiltrate universities, the media, the bureaucracy, and every other institution. Rightists believe, rightly or wrongly, that this plan was actually put into effect, and that this explains why university professors, media elites, civil servants, and so on tend to be left-wing today.1

One might imagine that the New Right would try to execute a similar long-term strategy to win back the culture. Indeed, right-wing movements have been known to do something like this — the Federalist Society has been able to keep the American judiciary in rough ideological balance.

But the Federalist Society is part of the old conservative movement; the New Right has not shown much interest in executing a long-term strategy of institutional capture. Instead, they put most of their eggs in the basket of the Trump presidency, apparently hoping that either Trump would win the whole culture for them in a few years, or that he’d turn America into some kind of quasi-dictatorship that allowed his successors to continue the project of culture war and race war into the indefinite future. In terms of direct cultural appeal, the New Right mostly limited themselves to shouting online.

This demonstrates the extreme impatience of the New Right. Part of this is probably just inherent to rightist movements in general — there’s a reason that they’re called “reactionary”. Rightism tends to be strongly motivated by fear — the conceit is usually that if extreme measures are not taken right now, everything good in the world will be destroyed. The belief in imminent destruction doesn’t exactly lend itself to a patient long-term strategy of institutional takeover.

But part of the reason has to be the movement’s online roots. For people whose defining cultural expression consists of memes and Twitter mobs, the strategy of patiently infiltrating PhD programs over the course of 30 years must sound like hell. Virality and online conflict give instant gratification; winning a presidential election is only slightly less instantaneous. Institutional takeover requires a patience that was definitely present in 1985 among sad-sack leftist grad students with nothing to lose, but is in short supply among today’s online politics junkies.

This is why when Trump fades from the political scene and fails to be replaced by an eternal dynasty of rightist caudillos, the New Right will feel like they have nothing.

#### The New Right couldn’t make alliances

Politics is the art of making strategic alliances. The old conservative movement was very effective at this. Uniting the interests of Christian conservatives and libertarians took some doing. And conservatives [worked heroically to include Catholics](https://accc4truth.org/2018/11/20/the-doctrine-of-co-belligerence/) in a movement once dominated only by Protestants, leading to the Reagan Revolution and the exodus of Italian, Polish, and Irish voters from the Democrats to the GOP.

MAGA itself made strategic alliances in its successful 2024 comeback campaign. Co-opting RFK, Jr. — formerly a well-known progressive — into the fold was detrimental to the nation, but was also a stroke of political genius. Trump even allied with Tulsi Gabbard, using their shared fondness for Russia.

Trump’s 2024 campaign also offered the GOP its chance for the biggest ethnic realignment since Reagan. Trump won primarily thanks to the exodus of large numbers of [Hispanic and Asian voters](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/what-drove-asian-and-hispanic-voters) from the Dems to the GOP. These voters were frustrated by “woke” progressive attitudes toward race, and swayed by Trump’s promises to tame inflation.

But no sooner had these nonwhite voters handed Trump the presidency than the New Right started attacking them. From Bo French’s anti-Indian rants to Stephen Miller’s encouragement of racial profiling in ICE raids, rightists in power spit on the very people they needed in order to build long-lasting support. Meanwhile, rightist intellectuals continued to say dismissive and mean things about minority voters:

This spectacular failure to repeat Reagan’s conversion of “white ethnics” will come back to haunt the right in the future. Already, many Hispanic Trump supporters [shifted back to the Dems](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/06/latino-voters-midterms-republicans-trump) in the midterms, while others stayed home in disgust.

As I wrote in a post back in September, this tendency to attack and exclude potential allies will ultimately doom the New Right:

> It’s this pathological inability to understand alliances and coalition-building that will ultimately doom the New Right…[T]his is a movement built to exclude and divide and splinter — both because of the querulous personalities of rightists themselves, and because of the intransigence of a racial ideology that [abhors any impurity](https://x.com/MegaBasedChad/status/2099557616708112711). If they ever managed to see off the Hispanics and the Asians, the rightists would start in on the Greeks and the Italians, and so on. There’s no victory in sight — only eternal conflict. [These are not nation-builders](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/this-thing-will-fail); they are nation-dismantlers.

Ultimately, I think this tendency probably also flows from the New Right’s online origins. On platforms like Twitter/X, attention is the only currency that matters, and denouncing people gets more attention than patiently building durable alliances.

#### The sales pitch to young men was fundamentally flawed

Right-wing movements have always appealed to men by portraying themselves as more manly than their opponents. Trump and MAGA had many different appeals to masculinity, including winning the favor of “podcast bros” like Joe Rogan who had the ears of many American men. That was smart, and had the potential to be durable.

But the New Right [often appealed to men by promoting “incel” ideas](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2024/aug/05/young-men-voters-us-election-trump-harris). For those who are unacquainted with incel ideology, the idea is that if women are free to choose their own partners, all the women will go for a few highly desirable men (“chads”), leaving the vast majority of men celibate and frustrated. The New Right married this idea to anti-feminist politics — it promised to reduce women’s status and independence in society, in order to force them to accept lower-status men as partners, thus making the distribution of sex more egalitarian.

The spread of incel ideas among the New Right explains the recent rightist uproar over the part of Grand Theft Auto 6 in which you have to buy flowers for your girlfriend:

The idea is that in a society free of progressive values, men would never have to woo women by buying them flowers or doing nice things for them; they would just demonstrate their superior status and power as men, and women would offer themselves up. (Apparently these rightists know little or nothing about courtship in the 19th century, or the 1950s, but that’s beside the point.)

This absurd message had more appeal than you might expect. Sexual frustration is a powerful motivator for many naive young men, and the idea that right-wing politics could lead to more sexual success was a seductive one. The only problem with this is that it *wasn’t actually true* — or at least, there wasn’t enough truth in the story to actually make a difference to men’s lives. If you couldn’t get a date in 2024, you couldn’t get a date in 2026 either.

I suspect that there is only so long that you can appeal to men by calling them sexless losers. It only takes most of them a short time to wake up and realize that supporting right-wing politicians has no chance of improving their sex lives, now or 20 years from now. By 2026, young men’s flirtation with the political right was ending:

Source: NYT via [Derek Thompson](https://x.com/DKThomp/status/2123489118642659662)

Source: NYT via [Derek Thompson](https://x.com/DKThomp/status/2123489118642659662)

These numbers are partially due to differential turnout; a lot of former Trump supporters simply stayed home in 2026. But withdrawing in disgust is also a way of showing a lack of support. The New Right’s message to young men — crafted for an extremely online audience, in order to get attention in online forums filled with frustrated young rejects — simply didn’t have what it takes to hold the attention or retain the allegiance of America’s young men.

#### The New Right is fundamentally parasitic on Western Civilization

The online world is an ephemeral place. Attention comes and goes, the news cycle turns over, memes become boring and stale. A social movement that arises from this impermanent space will inevitably have difficulty carrying out any change that requires more than a couple of years. Thus it was with the New Right. [I wrote back in 2025](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/this-thing-will-fail) that the Trump movement itself was destined to be ephemeral, because it built no lasting institutions:

> Trump’s movement has been around for a decade now, and in all that time it has built absolutely nothing. There is no Trump Youth League. There are no Trump community centers or neighborhood Trump associations or Trump business clubs. Nor are Trump supporters flocking to traditional religion; Christianity has [stopped declining](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/) since the pandemic, but both Christian affiliation and church attendance remain [well below](https://news.gallup.com/poll/642548/church-attendance-declined-religious-groups.aspx) their levels at the turn of the century. Republicans still [have more children](https://ifstudies.org/blog/the-trump-bump-the-republican-fertility-advantage-in-2024) than Democrats, but [births in red states have fallen](https://ifstudies.org/blog/where-are-the-babies-in-red-states-fertility-rates-are-higher) too.
> In Trump’s first term, the attempts at organized civic participation on the Right were almost laughably paltry. A few hundred Proud Boys got together and went to brawl with antifa in the streets of Berkeley and Portland. There were a handful of smallish right-wing anti-lockdown protests in 2020. About two thousand people rioted on January 6th — mostly people [in their 40s and 50s](https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2022/01/03/jan-6-rioters-white-older). And none of these ever crystallized into long-term grassroots organizations of the type that were the norm in the 1950s.
> For a very few people, the first Trump term was a live-action role-playing game; for everyone else, it was a YouTube channel.
> And in Trump’s second term so far? Nothing. Even [the rally numbers are way down](https://ash.harvard.edu/articles/the-real-numbers-tracking-crowd-sizes-at-presidential-rallies/). National conservatives who might have gone out to meet each other in 2017 are hunkering at home alone in their living rooms, swiping back and forth between X and OnlyFans and DraftKings, pumping their fists in the air as they read about how Elon Musk [is] firing people or Trump is cutting off aid to Ukraine. “You can just do things”, except almost zero of Trump’s supporters are actually doing anything except passively cheering for their notional team…[T]he thumos is all secondhand.
> The MAGA movement, you see, is an internet thing. It’s another [vertical online community](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/vertical-communities) — a bunch of deracinated, atomized individuals, thinly connected across vast distances by the notional bonds of ideology and identity. There is nothing in it of family, community, or rootedness to a place. It’s a digital consumption good. It’s a subreddit. It is a fandom.

I don’t think I’d change a word of that.

The New Right claims to be the champions of Western Civilization, but in fact their movement is a parasite on the actual Western Civilization that birthed them. They are not the kind of people who could ever build Notre Dame; they could only post memes of Notre Dame to win a fleeting argument on the internet.

The real bones of Western Civilization — the things that have always made it mighty — are its *institutions*. They are courts, corporations, bureaucracies, markets, churches, universities, charities, armies, and so on. They are fundamentally cooperative, long-lasting, constructive things. They require great cooperation to build, and they work by fostering ongoing, productive cooperation among the people who sustain them.

The New Right are not institution-builders; they are institution-mockers. They are squalling children, cradled in the bosom of Western Civilization, shaking their tiny fists and throwing a tantrum because they were asked to do real work to sustain their priceless inheritance. Throwing a tantrum because someone asked them to court women with flowers. Throwing a tantrum because someone expected them to work alongside industrious Indian engineers. Throwing a tantrum because they didn’t like the color of the faces they saw at a football game they didn’t even attend. Tantrums as a lifestyle, tantrums as a video game, tantrums as the ultimate form of decadent, useless consumption.

No civilization will ever be built, or rebuilt, by the hands of such men.

But it would be arrogant to believe that the New Right are unique in this regard. The woke movement of the 2010s built more offline institutions than the New Right did, but ultimately proved more interested in dismantling every facet of American culture and society. The leftist movement of the 2020s is barely less online than the New Right, and even more focused on tantrums as the praxis of change.

Social media has given us the ability to spend our entire lives playing a video game that looks like reality. “Press A to throw tantrum.” Almost everything that looks like a movement these days is simply the spectacle of a large mass of consumers playing these video games and calling it politics. The real, hard, slow work of building institutions is still being done, to some extent, but the people doing it are not the people dunking on you on X, or ranting for attention on TikTok, or filling the ears of D.C. staffers with nonsense and poison.

title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
subtitle: For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reap…
feedText: Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes. When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been li…
articleBody:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science [Margaret Rossiter](https://sts.cornell.edu/margaret-rossiter) coined[the term “The Matilda Effect”](https://www.openculture.com/2025/12/matilda-effect.html) to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film *[Hidden Figures](https://amzn.to/2HTG1jS) * have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, [in footnotes](https://www.openculture.com/2019/02/womens-hidden-contributions-to-modern-science-get-revealed-by-new-study.html).

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “[Floating University](https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html)” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the[Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) [in Physics](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the [Sorbonne](https://www.sorbonne-universite.fr/en/university/history-and-heritage/history), the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site [Famous Scientists](https://www.famousscientists.org/marie-curie/), “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the [French Academy of Sciences](https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/). It would take another 51 years before the first woman, [Marguerite Perey,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Perey) a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more [influential scientists](https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/read-the-dont-let-the-bastards-get-you-down-letter-that-albert-einstein-sent-to-marie-curie-during-a-time-of-personal-crisis-1911.html) and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and [only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-the-nobel-prizes-missing-female-scientists/?redirect=1), out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making [major contributions to chemistry](https://www.thoughtco.com/famous-women-in-chemistry-609453). Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

title: Driving Leg
subtitle: While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his…

articleBody:
While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his feet scuttled side-to-side on the bumpy field, as he tried to position him perfectly. It was his birthday, and we were playing a celebratory game with our extended family at his parents’ house an hour away from ours. After triumphantly catching the ball, he collapsed abruptly to the ground and, when we rushed over, he immediately told me to take him to the ER because he knew a bone had broken. I hate to admit that one of the first things I looked at—silently, selfishly—was which leg was hurt.

Right leg. Driving leg. At that moment, I knew that I was in for what my therapist friend would later call a “growth opportunity.”

Up until that point, my husband had done all of the driving for our family of four, us and our 13-year-old twins; I pinch-hit only when he went out of town. Living previously in Beijing, Brooklyn, and then downtown Boston had obviated most any need to drive, and my skills were basic anyhow, as my immigrant parents had severely limited my mobility as a suburban teenager. In the decade since moving to Cambridge and buying a car, my slight fear of being behind the wheel had deepened into a full-on phobia. The road seemed increasingly like a slippery sheet of ice, unpredictable and dangerous, and I clung to public transit, which is better in Boston than in most American cities though far from comprehensive.

I had always maintained that being terrified to drive in greater Boston was a rational response. Based on accident statistics, Allstate has ranked Boston as America’s worst city for drivers for eleven straight years. There is the running of red lights, the “banging” of “ueys,” the weaving through former-cow-path streets, the traffic jams, the rush hour daredevilry, the cutting off, the honking, the flicking off, the jaywalking, the lawless bicycling, the urgency, the rage, the tailgating. Indeed, it was this last behavior that set me off more than any other. I can picture it now: the heat in my rearview mirror, the voice inside my head that said, *You’re going too fuckin’ slow, you’re a pathetic driver, you need to get out of my way and off the road, you don’t deserve to be here—oh look, an Asian woman, of course.*

Unfortunately, the porous emotional boundaries that had served me well to date as a writer were terrible for a driver. Every time I got behind the wheel, I felt squeezed by the time-is-money capitalist python and crushed down by the country’s sexism and racism; the entire experience of being seen, judged, and honked at was psychologically harrowing. My cringing fear translated into a self-abasing timidity, and I let every single person who wanted to cut in front of me cut. Flash, flash; flash, flash.

After the ER trip that put my husband’s broken fibula in a temporary cast, I managed to pilot the car the hour home on the highway. After his surgery, he was ordered to keep weight off the foot for at least a month, and I prepared to take over the driving. Weekend drum and tennis lessons, weeknight capoeira lessons. I was finally going to learn to drive in Boston.

My instinct on my first drive was to flick loving-kindness at all the other drivers around me as I drove. *May you be happy—and you—and you—and you—and you.* This was a practice I’ve had on and off for the past two decades, ever since I sat my first weeklong silent retreat at the Insight Meditation Society, a loving-kindness focused program led by vipassana teacher Michele McDonald, who counseled us to take a light approach. If you’re sitting on the subway, you can just flick [metta](https://tricycle.org/magazine/metta-practice/) quickly at people, one by one, she said. You don’t have to make it something big and serious. I was living in New York at the time, and it was easy to feel barricaded or hostile or shrunken, especially when crammed into the tin can of the subway with strangers, and flicking loving-kindness at fellow riders shifted something in me—it expanded me, softened me, softened the space between me and others, woke me to the present. When I did the same while driving, it worked similarly, creating a radiant force field through which all the cars moved and related to one another. I could impute positive intentions to drivers I’d read earlier as only erratic, selfish, or terrifying. Even when confronted with impatience and rage, through the practice I learned that those feelings did not have to become mine. Each time I drove, my mind grew quieter.

Of all of the categories of people one can send loving-kindness to (self, benefactor, friend, neutral, difficult), I’ve always found the self the hardest, or at least I’ve found it hard to receive my own good intentions, but in this time of forced growth, I had to try. I returned to the [Metta Bhavana](https://dharmaseed.org/talks/3512/): *May I be safe, may I be peaceful.* In this mindset, when I had to make a turn, I realized that I didn’t have to peel out in front of oncoming traffic in a death-defying manner, no matter what the person behind me insisted. I could simply wait until there was a gap in traffic or someone let me go. And they did. There’s actually a lot of kindness out on the roads, in moments people do seem to understand that we’re suffering through this abominable system together and a little kindness can shift the whole system. These kindnesses, and my own, enabled me to enter the slipstream of humanity as an equal. Before, I used to flash my lights, urging others to turn out of terror, but slowly and through practice, I began to do it mainly to be part of the web of the road. I’ve become more confident about driving exactly how I want; after all, these roads are my roads too. And I admit that on some days I do hit the gas instead of flashing my lights because there are places I need to get to on time too.

In retrospect, I see I used the loving-kindness practice to recreate the conditions of bicycling in China, a practice that also began in terror when I moved there in my early 20s but soon became one of my favorite parts of living there. The crucial difference in the driving cultures is that in China, two decades ago at least, driving was incorrigibly social, with cars and bicycles and pedestrians maintaining an exquisite awareness of the world around them, like stars accommodating one another in a jellied, shifting constellation. By contrast, driving in the U.S. is a deeply antisocial activity, everyone zooming around mindlessly as if they are the sun around which the entire roadway universe should revolve. The Chinese view is closer to the Buddhist one, where we are not individuals full of a separate self-nature but instead are waves in a vast, interdependent ocean of being. Nowhere in the world more vividly demonstrates to me the idea that life arises from innumerable and interconnected causes and conditions beyond our control than the wild roadways of greater Boston.

Nowhere in the world more vividly demonstrates to me the idea that life arises from innumerable and interconnected causes and conditions beyond our control than the wild roadways of greater Boston.

A month after the fibula break, metta had helped me muster up the courage to do the routine drives, but I still hadn’t mastered getting back on the highway or parallel parking or crossing the river into Boston proper, and I still struggled with dread when I was scheduled to drive. Recently, in preparation to fetch my son from a sleepover at his friend’s house during a nor’easter, I tried to give myself a panicked crash course in the confuddling cuneiform of the windshield wipers, but when I pictured accidentally turning on the high beams instead, and subsequently crashing, I allowed myself to chicken out and ask the friend’s dad, a much more experienced driver than I, if he would be willing to drive my son back, and he did.

My husband recently got his cast off and is now in a boot, but the doctor prescribed yet another month of keeping weight off his foot and then another two weeks of walking with the boot, and then we’ll see. The night we found out, I had a nightmare: I was driving a car that was hurtling at top speed down a highway in New Jersey at night, my husband and our best friends in the car, but I was shocked to find myself steering from the middle of the back seat. As I struggled to follow the arcane directions on Google Maps, I yelled out for help to the men in the front seat, only to find that they were both fast asleep. Then I heard my friend next to me hollering at me to stay awake, but I couldn’t, my eyes kept dropping closed, and I could hear car horns faintly through my drowsy haze as the car drifted all over the highway. I jolted awake. I interpret this dream to mean that at this moment, I feel both in control and out of control, which is not a bad description of driving, and of life. While having no power over the mighty ocean, when awash in its convulsions, the wave called “I” does have some choice in how to incline its mind. Before I turn the key each time, I remind myself: flick, flick, flick; flick, flick, flick.

articleBody:
The [MusicTech Magazine](https://musictech.com/magazine) November/December 2026 issue goes on sale this week, bundled with *NME Magazine*. Here’s how you can get a copy.

Last April, we announced [the relaunch of the MusicTech print edition](https://musictech.com/news/industry/musictech-returns-to-print-after-5-years-in-a-new-premium-magazine-format/) after a four-year hiatus, and we’ve since had [Blake Slatkin](https://musictech.com/artists/blake-slatkin/), [Sudan Archives](https://musictech.com/artists/sudan-archives/), [KÁRYYN](https://musictech.com/artists/karyyn/) and [DJ_Dave](https://musictech.com/artists/dj_dave/) grace the print cover. Now, we’re gearing up to launch the November/December 2026 issue, which will as always come bundled with a copy of *NME Magazine*.

Mark your calendars for Thursday November 26 at 2pm GMT – that’s when the cover stars of both magazines will be revealed and the mags go on sale exclusively via retailer Dawsons. [The waiting room is open](https://www.nme.com/magazine), so check it out now.

Besides *MusicTech*, [Guitar.com](https://guitar.com/) has also returned to print. *Guitar.com*, *MusicTech* and *NME* are sister publications under NME Networks. The new *Guitar.com* and *MusicTech* print editions alternate with every bi-monthly edition of *NME Magazine* – which itself was relaunched in 2023 – meaning three print editions per calendar year for each brand.

[Subscribe here for more information about MusicTech Magazine](http://eepurl.com/jiVdGs) and to receive an exclusive queue jump opportunity, where readers can get their hands on a copy before anyone else. *MusicTech* will send out queue jump tickets shortly before the magazine goes on sale to subscribers.
