title: AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage
subtitle: The fake footage doesn’t match official photos of the bridge, and Google says the clip contains a SynthID watermark.
feedText: A video shows damage caused to the Crimean Bridge after Ukrainian strikes in November 2026. This video isn’t real and was made with AI. A viral video supposedly showing damage to the Crimean Bridge after it was attacked by Ukraine in November 2026 isn’t real and was made with AI. The structure in the fake clip doesn’t match the real bridge, and Google’s SynthID detector told us the video contained an invisible SynthID watermark which suggests that it was made or edited with Google AI. The video has been 'liked' thousands of times online. It was first shared by an Instagram account on 16 November with claims it showed the damage caused by an initial drone attack .
articleBody:
# AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage – Full Fact

## AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage

## What was claimed

A video shows damage caused to the Crimean Bridge after Ukrainian strikes in November 2026.

## Our verdict

False. This video isn’t real and was made with AI.

A viral video supposedly showing damage to the Crimean Bridge after it was attacked by Ukraine in November 2026 isn’t real and was made with AI.

The structure in the fake clip doesn’t match the real bridge, and Google’s SynthID detector told us the video contained an invisible SynthID watermark which suggests that it was made or edited with Google AI.

The video has been 'liked' thousands of times online. It was first shared by an Instagram account on 16 November with claims it showed the damage caused by an initial drone attack .

The first attack on 16 November reportedly damaged the arch over the road section of the bridge, but the fake footage does not match what the real bridge looks like.

Join 75,000 newsletter subscribers who trust us to check the facts

Our fact checks are free to read but not to produce, so you will also get occasional emails about fundraising and other ways you can help. You can unsubscribe at any time. For more information about how we use your data see our Privacy Policy .

The fake version shows two road bridges. In reality , one of the bridges is a rail bridge . The real rail bridge arch also has a distinct criss-cross pattern on the lowest rung near the track that isn’t present in the fake version.

Ukraine attacked the bridge, which links occupied Crimea to Russia, again on 17 November, severing the road bridge , and on 19 November , reportedly damaging the rail bridge too.

Again, official photos of the damage caused by these later strikes do not match the fake video circulating online.

It can be difficult to tell the difference between real and AI-generated videos, particularly when they circulate after real events. Our misinformation toolkit can help you become more confident to spot AI-generated content.

title: A Salesman’s Last Pitch
subtitle: At the September 2026 Republican convention in Dallas, and then from  MAGA rally to  MAGA rally, Donald Trump announced that everyon…
feedText: Well, the votes are in. By any measure, by any geographic survey, whether looking at federal or state elections, whether looking at  the west coast or the east coast, or the midwest, or the north or the south, or the states outside the continental United States, or red states or blue states, the midterm election results proved to be a devastating national rebuke of Trump far exceeding the expectations of any pundit or prediction market. articleBody:
At the September 2026 Republican convention in Dallas, and then from  MAGA rally to  MAGA rally, Donald Trump announced that everyone should vote as if he were on the midterm ballots. Well, the votes are in. By any measure, by any geographic survey, whether looking at federal or state elections, whether looking at  the west coast or the east coast, or the midwest, or the north or the south, or the states outside the continental United States, or red states or blue states, the midterm election results proved to be a devastating national rebuke of Trump far exceeding the expectations of any pundit or prediction market.

On November 5, two days after election day, I visited online trumpstore.com, the retail outlet of The Trump Organization. This is where you can buy Trump branded merchandise.  The site declared there was an early Black Friday sale—50 % off. Trump martini glasses. Trump bras. Trump sportswear. Trump sneakers. Trump hats. Trump candles. Trump honey. Trump coffee.

But missing were such things as Trump steaks, Trump $100,000 watches, Trump  gold colored cell phones and Trump wine. Even missing was the Trump God Bless the USA Bible (King James version, printed in China, tariff exempt, costing $3 to print and retailing for $59.99).

All these items, wherever they can be found, remain a  haunting reminder that before Donald Trump was a politician, he was always a salesman. And the product to be sold was always the same. The product was Donald J. Trump.

Trump will always be selling that product. But now there will be far fewer customers. The midterm elections may mark the end to the best of Trump’s salesmanship days.

Polls show that Trump is perceived, by even those in the MAGA camp, to have lost power within the GOP. His attempt a few days after the election to suggest on Truth Social that the elections were rigged  was widely ignored but even semi-fellow traveler Megyn Kelley dismissed this sales pitch with undisguised contempt. (On November 19, Trump acknowledged that Democrats won the House and the Senate.)

JD Vance also got in the act. He pronounced the reason why so many Republicans were swept out to oblivion in a blue wave was because of Iran, affordability, and Israel, a not too subtle dig at the Trump administration’s agenda and record. To rub it in, Vance said about  the decision to go to war with Iran: “If you like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so.” Surprisingly, almost shockingly, Trump at first did not slap Vance down; he even implied he went along with the diagnosis.

Not surprisingly Trump later distanced himself from the midterms Republican disaster. The problem, he said in an interview on Sixty Minutes and elsewhere, was that his name was not on the ballot. What is laughable is almost pathetic in its justice. There is no Trump the triumphant. Instead we have Trump the lame duck who ducks blame.

Alarmingly, what is also becoming more obvious to more people, there is something wrong with him. His rambling speech on the eve of the November 3rd election before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was noted for its bizarreness. The major portion of the speech was on the pool itself, and its purported history of disrepair and decay. It could almost be taken as a soliloquy that symbolizes the state of his administration and, for that matter, of himself.

Some have noticed discolorations and apparent needle marks on his hands covered up ineffectively with make-up. Others have commented on how he falls asleep in public. It has been reported that in his second term, he has fallen asleep in public at least 29 times, and  most recently he fell asleep in public in a meeting with Putin and Xi. Some claim it appears he has even  briefly nodded off while standing when others were speaking. His disjointed public comments on how he aesthetically appreciated the shape of a male senator’s ass raised eyebrows. None of this is a good look for a salesman.

There are parallels  between Trump and Arthur Miller’s  salesman, Willie Loman, in the play “Death of a Salesman”:  the tawdriness, the narcissism, the amorality,  the self-delusion, the decline. But ultimately Trump is no Willie Loman. Loman ended up broke and buried in obscurity. Instead, Trump has demonstrated an astounding phoenix like resilience in rising out of the ashes of his own making.  Whether its six bankruptcies, failed casinos and airlines enterprises, a taped admission on how he likes to grab women by their private parts, a payout of hush money to a porn star, a jury finding him liable for sexual assault, a jury handing out 34 felony convictions for fraud, or a failed  attempt to overthrow the election of a president by lies and mob violence, he emerges somehow intact. And  each time he rises we all end up talking about him. He even gets re-elected president.

Maybe this time it’s different. This time Trump smells of decay and corruption. The one  who promised  to drain the swamp is now seen bathing in it. Formerly vociferous MAGA supporters have turned on Trump over Epstein. Polling has shown that topping even issues of affordability and an unpopular war with Iran, is the issue of corruption. In less than in two years in his second term, Trump’s net worth has gone up by three billion. Millions may be paid out to his crypto enterprise with presidential pardons to follow. Family and friends get wealthier too. Billionaires curry favor by paying out millions to his causes, such as for a ballroom to replace a wing of the White House wiped out by his wrecking ball.

In the midterm elections Trump gave his sales pitch that he should be considered to be on the ballot. Now he faces  rock bottom approval ratings  and a Congress dominated by Democrats voter instructed to turn things around and stand firm against his failed agendas. With an  election outcome paralleling Vicktor Orban’s  overwhelming election defeat last April, it is likely Trump as salesman has transitioned to involuntary retirement. Who will listen to his pitches?  Not a Congress that was elected to oppose him. Not the great majority of voters that rebuked him. His last pitch in the midterms will prove to be precisely that, his last sales pitch.

So Trump may now have to turn to his other master role, the role of a bully. Trump remains president and holds immense power. Instead of backing down, his appointment of Stephen Miller as his chief of staff signals Trump may be spoiling for a fight. Miller has endorsed threats from Trump administration lawyers that they may criminally prosecute members of Congress for investigating  or threatening to investigate the administration. But such legally ludicrous threats display desperation, not strength.

Trump’s threats to veto bills  from the new Democratic Congress also threatens  Republicans in Congress  facing re-election in 2028 as well as the presidential aspirations of Rubio, Vance and others. As more vetoes pile up, Republican members of Congress  will face the no-win situation on whether or not to vote to override any of the vetoes. Motivated by political survival, some Republicans may muster the resolve to defy Trump.

In the meantime, Trump’s judicial and other nominations will likely flounder, making Trump look weak and ineffectual. The Democratic controlled  Congress will conduct investigations that will inevitably uncover more scandals and stunning examples of incompetence. This Congress will control the purse strings and the  appropriations process over projects like White House ball rooms and ICE detention camps.  Courts overall will continue to rule against him. And Trump’s appearance of physical and mental deterioration will continue, becoming  harder to cover up or deny.

Yet it is worth remembering Trump has defied the odds every time when it looked like he had no way out. Will Trump rise out of the ashes once again?  Will  Democrats unwittingly find a way to reap defeat from their current victory?

Buckle up, we may be in for quite a ride.

subtitle: Nach mehr als zwei Jahren Pause belebt Apple seine traditionsreiche (PRODUCT)RED-Reihe offenbar wieder.
feedText:

articleBody:
**Nach mehr als zwei Jahren Pause belebt Apple seine traditionsreiche (PRODUCT)RED-Reihe offenbar wieder. Wie der Bloomberg -Reporter Mark Gurman (via MacRumors ) berichtet, bereitet der Konzern für Anfang Dezember zwei neue Sondereditionen vor: den erst kürzlich erschienenen HomePod mini 2 sowie die AirPods Max 2.**

Die Ankündigung soll pünktlich zum Welt-AIDS-Tag am 1. Dezember 2026 erfolgen – passend zum 20-jährigen Jubiläum der Organisation (RED).

## Knallrot beim Lautsprecher, überraschend dezent beim Kopfhörer

Optisch geht Apple bei den beiden Audio-Produkten sehr unterschiedliche Wege: Der kompakte Smart-Speaker erhält dem Bericht [nach](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-23/apple-s-new-airpods-max-homepod-mini-2-to-get-product-red-release-for-holidays) ein durchgehend rotes Netzgewebe und ergänzt damit die fünf bisherigen Standardfarben (Weiß, Rosa, Grün, Blau und Mitternacht). Technisch bleibt alles unverändert.

Bei den Over-Ear-Kopfhörern verzichtet Apple demnach auf ein komplett rotes Gehäuse. Stattdessen feiern die Kopfhörer die Rückkehr der Farbe Silber kombiniert mit weißen Ohrpolstern und einem weißen Kopfbügel. Einziger roter Akzent ist die Digital Crown an der Oberseite.

## Erste (PRODUCT)RED-Hardware seit 2023

Aktuell führt Apple keinerlei (PRODUCT)RED-Hardware oder -Zubehör mehr im Sortiment. Die letzten roten Geräte waren das [iPhone 14 (2022)](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/iphone-15-vs-iphone-14-aktuelles-lineup-verkauft-sich-schwaecher-als-vorgaenger/) sowie die [Apple Watch Series 9 (2023)](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/rote-apple-watch-bringt-apple-bald-product-red-uhren/). Ein Teil der Erlöse aus dem Verkauf der Sondereditionen fließt traditionell an den Global Fund zur Bekämpfung von AIDS.

Neben den beiden Audio-Geräten arbeitet Apple laut Gurman zudem an weiterem rotem Zubehör, darunter ein neues Sportarmband für die Apple Watch sowie eine rote Trageschlaufe für AirPods. Offizielle Preise für die Sondereditionen sind noch nicht bekannt, dürften sich aber an den regulären Preisen (169 Euro für den HomePod mini 2 bzw. 579 Euro für die AirPods Max 2) orientieren.

articleBody:
Love time travel movies? You're not alone and, as a sci-fi staple, cinema has no shortage of timey-wimey greats. It's [Black Friday week](https://www.space.com/best-black-friday-deals-sales) and many of these titles are now deeply discounted. So, I picked out the ten time travel movies you need to own, from classic blockbusters like Back to the Future, through to modern gems such as Needle in a Timestack, where the only obstacle to time travel is your bank balance.

We do mean own, too. All too often, we've sat down to rewatch a film to find it's vanished from our streaming service. At best, it's rematerialized on a different streaming service; at worst, it's been exterminated as some media conglomerate's tax write-off. Even 'buying' a movie, you're just getting a license that can be revoked at any time.

The solution? By buying these time travel movies on Blu-ray or 4K UHD Blu-ray, they'll still be sitting on your shelf ready to watch and rewatch for years, even decades, from now.

title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
subtitle: Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month.
feedText:

articleBody:
Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month. Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica

Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

Kevin Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” Brooks Kraft/Getty Images

A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”

“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.

In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure.

In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug.

A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data.

Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”

Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”

## We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.

[↗ Primärquelle: propublica.org](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication.

[Share Your Experience](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “[creating a more predictable and transparent experience](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-authorization_progress.html)” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.

Last year Centene joined America’s largest insurers in vowing to rely on prior authorization less often. Industry representatives have said that the collective efforts of those insurers [will decrease their use of prior authorization across all of their plans by 11%](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/call_materials/priorauth-industry-reform-initiative-naic-rftf-6-29-26.pdf) in 2026. (Health plans aren’t required to publish 2026 data until next year.)

ProPublica sent Centene a detailed list of questions about its use of prior authorization and the impact it has on its customers. ProPublica also provided Ambetter with signed releases from customers, including Felicia, waiving their right to privacy, so that Centene representatives could speak with ProPublica about their specific denials. Centene didn’t respond to ProPublica’s questions. In a statement, a spokesperson for the company said that Ambetter is “committed to help ensure patients receive safe, appropriate, evidence-based care, and we continue to work to simplify the prior authorization process and reduce administrative burden for members and providers.”

Reached by phone, Counihan told ProPublica that he retired this year and declined to comment due to “contractual commitments” with the company that prevent him from doing so.

### Listen to Ambetter’s Then-CEO

Kevin Counihan tells a customer he can’t approve coverage of the treatment her doctor sought.

**Kevin Counihan:** I have taken this whole issue, uh, all the way through our medical directors and, uh, policy people and everywhere, and I’m — I’m sorry and disappointed to tell you that I don’t have approval to have this covered. Obtained by ProPublica

For some Ambetter customers, the consequences of prior authorization denials were particularly stark, leading to delayed tests and disrupted treatments. A small fraction of those customers got Ambetter to cover their care after complaining to powerful politicians. One Ambetter customer who was denied routine bloodwork complained to a state agency. Another who had been denied cancer treatment asked a U.S. senator for help.

Even though Felicia’s complaint made it all the way up to powerful politicians — and she had pressed Centene’s C-suite to get in touch — she was disheartened by what Counihan ultimately would have to say.

Felicia had lost track of all the hours spent on curbing her weight, going so far as to try three different anti-obesity medications. During the follow-up call, Counihan explained that didn’t actually have the authority to help with the fourth.

“Do what you need to do,” Counihan responded. “Escalate it in any way that you can.”

Jones at home with his 13-year-old daughter, Makenna Jones, as she plays the drums. He spent much of this year undergoing cancer treatment. Matt Odom for ProPublica

This spring, as Richie Jones recovered from having his tumor-filled prostate removed, he received some troubling news. The cancer was still in his body.

The 49-year-old drummer from Atlanta’s suburbs was willing to do anything to get more time with his wife and daughter. His oncologist said the best option was to shoot a pencil-sized beam of protons at the cancer that remained, zapping it out of existence. That kind of therapy can cost far more than standard radiation but inflicts far less damage to the rest of the body.

First, though, his oncologist had to confirm that Ambetter would cover proton therapy. He asked the insurer to approve it in advance, as it required. Ambetter denied the request based on a recommendation from an oncologist working with the insurer.

Insurers have varying policies on whether to cover proton therapy for patients with prostate cancer. In recent years, insurance researchers have found that patients with commercial plans who are facing a denial for proton therapy for a variety of cancers have a good shot of getting it overturned on appeal.

Jones’ oncologist appealed. That, too, was denied. Ambetter explained its decision in a letter to Jones, claiming he did “not have a type of cancer this treatment is used for.”

What angered Jones most was that there was a different doctor advising Ambetter on the denial of the appeal, and that doctor didn’t specialize in proton therapy, let alone cancer. It was an OB-GYN.

Fearful that his cancer would spread more, Jones emailed Ambetter’s support department, hoping to break through to whatever human was on the other end. “You have the power to allow my child to have her daddy around for years to come,” he wrote.

When people actually fight prior authorization denials, they have a good shot at winning. ProPublica’s analysis found that more than half of Ambetter customers who contested their denials had them overturned. But the vast majority of the time, denials go uncontested. Only 7% of prior authorization denials by Ambetter were challenged last year, the analysis found.

Marketplace plan holders told ProPublica that they didn’t appeal because they didn’t know about their rights or how to navigate the process. Insurance experts and advocates say that patience and persistence are required to fight a denial.

### Ambetter Customers Have a Good Shot at Overturning Their Denials. Few of Them Try.

Most prior authorization denials are never appealed. More often than not, Ambetter customers who appeal get approved after going through a complex process.

Source: ProPublica analysis of 2025 prior authorization disclosures from AuthDenied and insurance companies, including 21 Ambetter plans and 93 other plans. Figures from Wee People by ProPublica and Alberto Cairo. Brandon Roberts/ProPublica

On the other side of metro Atlanta from Jones, 48-year-old artist Travis Christopher was trying to get treatment for his liver cancer last year. After getting so sick that he left his job — and lost the insurance that came with it — he bought an Ambetter plan on the marketplace.

It covered a specialized treatment by his oncologist, who placed a wire of irradiated beads in his liver to precisely target his tumor. But to know if the radiation worked, his oncologist needed CT scans.

Ambetter denied three different requests for prior authorization for the scans. After a month of delays, Christopher complained to his state senator, saying that he was “stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.” The state senator passed it along to Georgia’s insurance commissioner. Soon after, Ambetter overturned the denial and agreed to cover the care.

Every day of delay can increase the odds that cancer spreads. No one can say how much the wait affected Christopher’s prognosis. What is certain is that Christopher’s health got worse in the months ahead. He died this past winter, shortly after his daughter was born.

Travis Christopher complained to his state senator that Ambetter had denied three requests for cancer scans. Courtesy of the Christopher family

Jones was able to get care in time. Like Christopher, he worked to draw attention to Ambetter’s denial. He contacted local journalists, wrote to the office of the U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, and filed a complaint with Georgia’s insurance commissioner. In late June, after getting in touch with staffers in both officials’ offices, Jones received a call from Emory Healthcare: Their oncologists were ready to start.

Ambetter had decided to reverse its denial.

Over the course of his nearly 40 rounds of proton therapy, Jones realized that he wanted others to know the importance of fighting back. So he granted permission to Ossoff to publish what had happened in a [report on prior authorization denials](https://www.ossoff.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/26.08.31_Sen.-Ossoff-Report%E2%80%94Insurance-Companies-Denying-Necessary-Health-Care.pdf). In a statement to ProPublica, Ossoff said that he has “heard from too many Georgians who get a cancer diagnosis, and then instead of being free to fight their cancer, they have to fight their insurance company.”

“We need to ban health insurance companies from denying or delaying needed health care,” Ossoff said in the statement.

Several months later, Jones stood in the lobby of Emory’s cancer center. Surrounded by his family and friends, he rang a ceremonial bell hanging on the wall, marking the end of his treatment.

It was only after he was in remission that Jones would begin to see just how much his complaint had mattered.

With Jones’ permission, ProPublica obtained records this month that shed light on why Ambetter changed its decision about the proton therapy. The records include a letter Ambetter sent to Georgia’s insurance commissioner’s office that explained the rationale for each of its denials. In the letter, the insurer wrote that it had decided, two days after Jones filed his complaint, to consult clinical guidelines used by America’s leading oncologists in determining how to proceed with covering his treatment. Ambetter previously had relied on a more restrictive guideline from a contractor that handles its prior authorization requests for cancer treatment.

“Why wasn’t that their guideline in the first place?” Jones said. “Why does it take being a squeaky wheel to have them change their mind?”

Jones at his drafting table in his art studio at home this month. He is a visual artist as well as a performer and percussion teacher. Matt Odom for ProPublica

In June 2025, following a meeting with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centene and other large insurers promised [to reduce the volume of medical services subject to prior authorization](http://ahip.org/news/press-releases/health-plans-take-action-to-simplify-prior-authorization). Centene has since touted “[measurable progress](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-authorization_progress.html)” toward fulfilling that promise. The company didn’t answer ProPublica’s questions about whether Ambetter’s prior authorization use has gone down this year.

But insurance experts, consumer advocates and lawmakers question how far those promises go.

Wendell Potter, a former Cigna executive turned consumer advocate, recently wrote that these commitments rely on “[an impressive-sounding number to mislead.](https://healthcareuncovered.substack.com/p/pr-stunt-unitedhealths-big-prior)” For instance, he said that UnitedHealthcare promised a 30% drop in prior authorization requirements, but only 2% of covered medical services are eligible for the more relaxed requirements. (UnitedHealthcare spokesperson Eric Hausman told ProPublica that the insurer has been “transparent” about its efforts to reduce the use of prior authorization and has already enacted some of them.)

Brit Vanneman, a staff attorney for the National Health Law Program, wrote that these commitments “[may simply be a strategic attempt to deflect growing public criticism](https://healthlaw.org/voluntary-industry-prior-authorization-commitments-empty-promises-little-accountability/)” regarding prior authorization.

“The commitments are vague,” Vanneman told ProPublica. “There’s a lot of fluff.”

What isn’t vague: the continued impact of prior authorization denials since the industry’s pledge.

> “I still do not have a CT scan scheduled, and am stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.”
> Travis Christopher, in an email to his state senator in September 2025

Two women got their denials overturned by Ambetter only after posting about them on social media. One, a Florida mother, told ProPublica she bought an Ambetter plan because her previous insurer stopped covering autism therapy for her 6-year-old son. The Ambetter plan she chose had covered other children seen by the providers who’d treated her son for the past two years. But Ambetter denied the request for his treatment this year, and her son’s care was put on pause.

The other, a Kansas woman, said Ambetter denied a drug infusion to treat her Crohn’s disease last year. She said this was shocking to her, since for the previous two years Ambetter had covered the infusion, which worked better for her than anything else she tried.

Both women’s social media posts prompted Ambetter reps to reach out to them directly, saying they wanted to address their problems. And indeed, the ordered treatments were provided.

Felicia wasn’t as fortunate. After Ambetter’s CEO expressed sympathy and encouraged her to fight for her obesity treatment, she moved forward with the final step in the process: asking an independent company to review her appeal.

At that point, Felicia had spent two years on three different weight-loss drugs that were covered by Ambetter, including the popular GLP-1 drug Ozempic. But those drugs had caused side effects, such as insomnia and migraines. When she was prescribed samples of tirzepatide, another GLP-1, by her doctor in 2023, everything finally clicked: She lost a significant amount of weight over two months without any side effects.

But Ambetter was not willing to cover Zepbound, the tirzepatide her doctor prescribed.

As a way to keep costs down, health insurers tend to deny requests for GLP-1s not listed on their formularies. When that happens, a customer can appeal and seek a formulary exception.

In September 2024, she asked her endocrinologist to support her appeal. He explained in a letter that a denial of this particular GLP-1 “could significantly hinder her progress and potentially lead to worsening of her condition, which could result in more intensive and costly interventions in the future.” As he saw it, this GLP-1 was “the most appropriate and potentially life-saving medication,” especially given Felicia’s other overlapping medical conditions.

But that November, the company overseeing the independent review declined to consider her appeal, writing that an appeal involving a medication that wasn’t on a health plan’s approved drug list was “outside of our scope of review.” In other words, Felicia had hit a dead end.

Felicia has continued struggling with obesity ever since the Zepbound denial. She’s also experienced worsening symptoms for several other chronic conditions, including persistent migraines. Felicia said she has nine each month on average, and medical experts say that obesity is a strong risk factor for migraines. But Ambetter has denied prior authorization for numerous migraine medications prescribed by her doctors.

Ambetter is the only insurance Felicia had ever bought. By this fall, she had become so fed up with the denials that she contacted an insurance broker to help her find another marketplace plan during open enrollment. But the quotes she received for various plans were either much higher than Ambetter’s or didn’t provide access to her doctors. If she wanted to clear the hurdles she’d faced, the cost would be far more than she could possibly afford.

It left her with a sinking feeling: Ambetter might be her only viable option.

## FL Studio 2026.2 Update und Sale

Bis zu 25 Effekt-Slots pro Mixer-Track bietet FL Studio 2026, sobald das angekündigte Update erscheint. Vorher gab es zehn und das war vielen Usern zu wenig. Ebenfalls neu ist hier die Option für absolutes Routing von nativen Plugins.

Außerdem wurde die Stem-Separation optimiert. Das Trennen von Audio in einzelne Parts funktioniert in der neuesten Version schneller, in der All Plugins Edition steht nun auch ein Modus mit sechs Stems bereit.

Die Toolbar und das Hauptmenü werden mit benutzerdefinierten Shortcuts erweitert. Patterns lassen sich schneller über „Split by Channel“ organisieren. Mit „Nebula“ gibt es zudem eine Art Karte oder Wolke, um Presets schneller zu entdecken.

FL Studio 2026.2 fügt zwei neue Plugins hinzu. PitchHiker ist für Tonhöhenkorrektur in Echtzeit zuständig, während es sich bei Pressure um einen neuen Stereo-Kompressor handelt.

Aktuell mach Image-Line auch einen Sale zum Black Friday, dabei kannst du ganz besonders bei der All Plugins Edition sparen, die 52 % günstiger ist. Bei Thomann gibt’s zusätzlich die Plugins Native Instruments Effects Series Mod Pack und AIR Music Technology Hybrid 3 kostenlos beim Kauf dazu. ## FL Studio 2026: Neuste Version der beliebten DAW

*[09. Juli 2026]* **FL Studio 2026 ist die neuste Version der beliebten DAW und kommt mit ein einigen Neuheiten im Gepäck. Dabei geht es unter anderem um den KI-Assitenten Gopher, der nun nicht nur Fragen beantwortet, sondern sogar Zugriff auf Funktionen der DAW bekommt. Und auch bei diesem Update gilt wieder, dass es für alle Nutzer kostenlos ist!**

Mit FL Studio 2026 veröffentlicht Image-Line ein umfangreiches Update für die Digital Audio Workstation. Im Rahmen der Lifetime-Free-Updates-Politik gibt’s die neuste Version wieder kostenlos für alle, die im Besitz einer Lizenz sind. Im Mittelpunkt stehen eine komplett überarbeitete Version des FLEX Instruments, neue KI-gestützte Funktionen, automatische Cloud-Backups und ein paar weitere Neuheiten.

FLEX wurde für FL Studio 2026 komplett überarbeitet · Quelle: Image-Line

Die größte Neuerung betrifft die vollständig überarbeitete Engine von FLEX. Das virtuelle Instrument verfügt nun über einen deutlich leistungsfähigeren Browser mit Suchfunktion über alle Sound-Packs hinweg. Dazu gehören erweiterte Filtermöglichkeiten inklusive Genre-Kategorien und eine schnellere Preset-Vorschau.

Gleichzeitig soll die neue Engine die CPU-Last bei zukünftigen Sound-Libraries spürbar reduzieren. Passend dazu erscheint die neue Core Series, die acht kostenlose Sound-Packs mit mehr als 200 Presets umfasst. Zudem werden Plugin-Grafiken jetzt in voller Größe dargestellt. Klasse!

Mit FL Cloud Project Backup führt Image-Line in FL Studio 2026 eine automatische Cloud-Sicherung für Projekte ein. Gespeicherte Projekte können direkt im FL-Cloud-Speicher gesichert werden und stehen so auch auf anderen Rechnern zur Verfügung. Und in kritischen Momenten werden die Nerven geschont!

Laut Hersteller werden sämtliche Backups verschlüsselt gespeichert und nicht zum Training von KI-Modellen verwendet. Abhängig vom gewählten FL-Cloud-Abo stehen zwischen 500 MB und 1 TB Speicherplatz zur Verfügung.

## Der Gopher KI-Assistent wird mächtiger

Der Gopher KI-Assistent bekommt in FL Studio 2026 auch direkten Zugriff auf DAW-Funktionen · Quelle: Image-Line

Außerdem spendiert FL Studio 2026 dem integrierten KI-Assistent Gopher einen Boost. Statt lediglich Fragen zu beantworten, kann Gopher nun aktiv in Projekte eingreifen. So organisiert das Tool auf Wunsch Spuren, richtet Mixer-Kanäle ein, passt Pegel und Plugin-Parameter an, erstellt Inhalte für die Piano-Rolle oder hebt Funktionen der Benutzeroberfläche hervor.

Diese Möglichkeiten sollen nicht nur Einsteigern den Umgang mit der DAW erleichtern, sondern ebenso bei erfahrenen Producern den Workflow beschleunigen. Auch hier betont Image-Line, dass keine Nutzerdaten zum KI-Training verwendet werden. Und ich muss sagen, dass dieses Feature sehr spannend aussieht und eigentlich gut in jede DAW passt.

Transmitter teilt Audio in Transienten- und Sustain-Anteile – sehr cool für Sounddesign · Quelle: Image-Line

Ebenfalls neu ist Transmitter, ein Plugin das Audiosignale in Transienten- und Sustain-Anteile aufteilt. Beide Signalbestandteile lassen sich anschließend unabhängig voneinander bearbeiten oder routen, was zusätzliche Möglichkeiten für kreatives Sounddesign eröffnet. Das Plugin ist Bestandteil der All Plugins Edition.

## Viele kleinere Verbesserung

Abonnenten von FL Cloud dürfen sich über eine deutlich erweiterte Loop Starter-Bibliothek mit zusätzlichen Loops und One-Shots aus verschiedenen Musikrichtungen freuen.

Und natürlich enthält FL Studio 2026 auch zahlreiche Bug-Fixes und Optimierungen. Das Chord Panel erkennt beispielsweise nun Akkorde und Noten in Echtzeit in der Piano-Rolle und erleichtert so das Arbeiten innerhalb einer Tonart. Piano-Roll-Noten lassen sich sogar individuell beschriften, um so Hinweise für das Arrangement oder eine Performance zu hinterlegen. Abgefahren!

- Einzelne Noten können in der Piano-Rolle jetzt beschriftet werden! · Quelle: Image-Line
- Neue Gain-Regler ermöglichen eine direkte Lautstärkeanpassung · Quelle: Image-Line

Neue Gain-Regler ermöglichen eine direkte Lautstärkeanpassung einzelner oder mehrerer Audio-Clips. Mit dem Audio Logger zeichnet FL Studio 2026 jetzt permanent die letzten 60 Sekunden des Master-Ausgangs auf, um spontane Ideen auch ohne aktivierte Aufnahmefunktion nachträglich zu sichern.

Insgesamt ein ziemlich rundes Update!

## Spezifikationen und Verfügbarkeit

Image-Line FL Studio 2026 läuft auf macOS und Windows. Die DAW bekommst du auch [hier bei Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/image-line_sequenzersoftware.html?offid=1&affid=84)*.

title: A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability
subtitle: For decades, astronomers have puzzled over whether a star’s given obliquity, or axial tilt, changes over time and space.

articleBody:
# A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star’s initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planets––stellar obliquity––holds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal , Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across “space” by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and “time” by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, says Biddle.

## Not A Lot Of Change

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We don’t see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

It is misaligned when the star’s spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a star’s tilt and the orbit’s tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

This artist's conception shows a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL

## Stellar Misalignments Are Out There

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, says Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets

But prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar system’s planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sun’s spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, says Biddle.

Biddle doesn’t know for certain if the Sun’s axis was tilted from the start.

But if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, says Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

## The Bottom Line?

There isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

### Sources:

Lauren Biddle

The Astronomical Journal

### Bruce Dorminey

Over the last three and a half decades, award-winning science journalist Bruce Dorminey --- a former Forbes senior science contributor, former Hong Kong Bureau Chief at Aviation Week and Space Technology magazine and former Paris-based technology correspondent for the Financial Times, has written for a multitude of high profile publications. They include Astronomy Magazine, Sky and Telescope, Scientific American, Science, Nature News, National Geographic, and Universe Today. He is the author of the 2001 book "Distant Wanderers: The Search for Planets beyond the Solar System." He was also the host of the "Cosmic Controversy" podcast which is still available via Podbean.

# A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star’s initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planets––stellar obliquity––holds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal , Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across “space” by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and “time” by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, says Biddle.

## Not A Lot Of Change

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We don’t see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

It is misaligned when the star’s spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a star’s tilt and the orbit’s tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

articleBody:
# ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?

T he kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling.

From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football.

“It’s so lovely to hear them,” said Alman, whose son is in year 5. “I used to hear them before Charlie was in there, and now I go out there and I know he’s one of them, and it’s really nice to see him playing. I’ll drive by there, and there’ll be a couple of footballs that have gone over the fence and rolled to the verge. They try to flag someone down to throw back the ball so the game’s back on. It’s the heartbeat of the village, you know.”

Gladestry is home to 400 people and sits (just) on the Welsh side of the border with England. Indeed, if you’ve ever walked the Offa’s Dyke footpath that runs, more or less, along that border, you’ll have passed right through the small cluster of buildings that mark its centre. The school has been educating Almans since Joseph’s grandfather and great-uncle arrived in 1917, but Charlie could be the last. In June, just before the start of the summer holidays, Powys county council announced that it wanted to close the school.

“It all seemed to come as a bit of a bolt out of blue,” said Alman. “We didn’t know nothing about it.” It was, however, just the latest episode in a slow-motion erosion of the foundations of life in mid-Wales, which is caused by generations of politicians failing to engage with an important question: how do you provide adequate services to a sparsely populated place if you’re not willing to spend more money? In other words, how do you solve a problem like Powys?

P owys was once a kingdom, from which Britain’s native population resisted the remorseless westwards expansion of the Anglo-Saxons for half a millennium or more. The kingdom disappeared in the 13th century, when the English conquered the last independent Britons, but seven centuries later – in 1974 to be precise – its name was dredged out of obscurity. (The word itself derives from pagus , the Latin word for countryside.)

At the time, the government in London was trying to rationalise local administration by combining smaller units into larger ones that were better able to meet the needs of their populations. The result was new inventions such as Greater Manchester, Avon, Humberside and Mid Glamorgan. A basic principle of the reform was that local authority areas needed at least 250,000 people to be viable. And this is where mid-Wales ran into trouble.

The existing counties of Breconshire, Radnorshire and Montgomeryshire were clearly too tiny to justify their continued administrative existence. Even combined into a single entity called Powys, however, the population was less than half the supposed minimum. “There are more sheepdog exemption licences than there are members of the population,” one peer said when the House of Lords debated the reform in 1972. “Powys, as we all recognise, is a county with too few people and too few resources,” said another.

There was no easy answer. The new county already covered 5,200 sq km (2,000 sq miles), and combining it with yet more parts of Wales risked creating something too unwieldy to be manageable. Merging it with anywhere in England was clearly unacceptable, so Powys was left as a vast underpopulated exception – its population density lower than any part of Britain south of the Highlands, its properties cumulatively worth less than any other county in England and Wales.

Mid-Wales is a unique place. Unlike other parts of Wales – with their coal, steel and slate – Powys was largely untouched by the industrial revolution. Much of the county lived by producing meat for export, sending its livestock to the market towns of England. As a result, in contrast to farming communities elsewhere in Wales, most of Powys is English-speaking, which means it’s linguistically cut off from rural areas to the north and west, and culturally distinct from places to the south.

It is unassuming, and it is beautiful; the kind of place that hippies such as my parents sought out in the 1970s when they wanted somewhere quiet to build a new kind of life. It is also empty. Even today, the county’s entire population – 135,000 – is barely equal to that of St Albans, yet it is spread over an area larger than Northumberland. That’s a quarter of Wales’s landmass with 4% of its population. If you were to add Powys’s two largest settlements together – Newtown, on the English border near Shrewsbury, and Ystradgynlais, 85km away in the Swansea valley – you still wouldn’t have enough people to reach the Office for National Statistics’ threshold for a “medium-sized town”.

It takes two and half hours to drive from one end of Powys to the other, from Eryri (Snowdonia) to the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons), though you might want to allow yourself more time in July, when visitors to the four-day agricultural jamboree that is the Royal Welsh Show throng the centre of the county; or in August, when caravans clog the county’s B-roads; or, at other times, in case of incidents on the A470.

The county is bumpy. It is for this reason that if you take a train between south and north Wales, you bypass Powys altogether and travel instead through the smooth green fields of England. That feels appropriate because, when it comes to Welsh politics, Powys residents feel ignored – as if their home county were just a blank between the electorally significant places above and below it.

“The truth is, civil servants in Cardiff have always viewed Powys as a nuisance,” one local politician told me recently. “We’re a policy nightmare, aren’t we? Hardly any people. Lots of sheep. We haven’t got a big city, we haven’t got a university, we haven’t got a general hospital. Miles and miles and miles of roads to maintain. We’re just very expensive.”

And this is why Gladestry Church in Wales primary school was slated for closure. It was not because of something it did or didn’t do, but because the council decided that it couldn’t afford it any more. “This is one of those papers that none of us like to have to present,” said James Gibson-Watt, the councillor responsible for education in Powys county council’s cabinet, when he formally proposed the closure at a council meeting in July, “but the numbers are very stark.”

M y family left the village 40 years ago, when our parents sold our farm, but our old teacher had told my brother Tom of the threat to the school, and Tom had told me, so we drove to Gladestry in September, when we heard that a public meeting had been called to discuss how the village could fight back against this threat to its future.

While we waited for everyone to file into the village hall, we reminisced about our own star turns on its stage. In December 1983, Tom had been Good King Wenceslas’ page, and I’d been Joseph, sinfully proud in dishcloth and dressing gown. Neither of us could quite remember why Wenceslas had been present at the birth of Christ.

Of the 100 or so people in attendance, probably everyone had at one time or another either performed on that stage, seen their children perform on it, or both. That’s what a school brings to a village: the one thing that everyone has in common. “We supported each other, we learned far more from each other than any lesson plan can provide, and that is what makes Gladestry school outstanding,” said one 17-year-old alumna, Eva Lloyd. Lloyd is the fourth generation of her family to pass through the school. Her speech was so eloquent she was immediately asked to repeat it, so it could be filmed and posted to the village Facebook page, which has 1,500 members – almost four times Gladestry’s population.

Inspectors from Estyn, the Welsh equivalent of Ofsted, published their most recent report into the school three years ago, and it could barely have been more glowing: pupils were proud of the school, they were well behaved, and their reading, maths and Welsh-language skills were impressive.

“That was 2023,” Hannah Price, who chairs the school governors, told me one evening over coffee after she’d finished her day’s work as a veterinary physiotherapist. “Mrs Beck [the head] sent four children to give the inspectors a guided tour and thought it would take them 10 minutes. Forty-five minutes later, she had to go and rescue the inspectors because they got shown every inch of the school with such, you know, animation and enthusiasm. It was all about the motto that we’re small but mighty, and how we won a maths competition, a cricket festival. They are amazing kids.”

But no matter how amazing these kids are, you can’t help but notice that there are very few of them. When the Estyn report was published, 40 pupils attended the school. By the time the council proposed closing it two and a half years later, there were only 31. The Welsh government’s definition of a small school is one with fewer than 91 pupils, so – with barely a third of that – Gladestry was very small indeed.

W elsh politics could, until the recent rise of Reform UK, be crudely but not unfairly caricatured as a battle between Labour in the south of the country and Plaid Cymru in the north and west. Powys is unique here too, and has in recent decades been more of a contest between the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats and an unruly gaggle of independents.

Although primary schools have been closing all over the country, particularly in London where the birthrate is low and house prices are high, the effect is particularly dramatic in a rural setting because distances are greater and there is often little else to bring a village together.

Parts of rural Scotland have also seen their schools close, but there councils wait until the pupil numbers are in single figures before taking action. Powys acts far sooner, and it is so cash-strapped that it can’t even afford to repurpose these shuttered buildings, which often still have sports facilities that everyone used to use. They are simply left to rot. At the closed schools of places such as Llanigon and Rhosgoch, the paint has lost its brightness, weeds have pushed up through the playground, ivy has climbed the walls.

“Nobody, nobody wants to see their local school closed. I mean, I don’t want to see Gladestry closed, I’d love to keep it,” said Gibson-Watt, who represents the Liberal Democrats, as we sat and talked in a cafe in Hay-on-Wye recently. “But when the report for the cabinet was prepared, there were 31 pupils there. There are now 23, and it’s projected to go to 19 in two years’ time. I mean, where do we draw the line?”

The trouble with primary schools is that, no matter how small they get, they will always need at least two teachers, as well as heat and light. There is always a minimum cost that can’t be reduced. The fewer pupils a school has, the more expensive each pupil becomes, which is tough when councils receive funding on a per-pupil basis. That means schools with surplus capacity are effectively being subsidised by the rest. Even before those extra pupils left, Powys county council was spending £7,696 a year to educate every child at Gladestry, compared with an average of £5,710 across the county as a whole. The school apparently also has, for what it’s worth, a maintenance backlog worth £184,452.

If you spend time reading the budget reports published by Powys county council, you can see why this is a problem. Year after year, the allocations it receives from Cardiff have failed to keep up with inflation, so the council has had to cut huge chunks from its budget – adding up to £100m over the past decade – to keep afloat. In the last financial year, the administration has budgeted to spend £379.3m, but that’s £12.3m more than it’s going to get, which means more cuts for this dwindling administrative machine. “It’s going to have to get a lot leaner again to survive, just to be solvent,” said Gibson-Watt.

Council officials expect they’ll need to cut another £40m from the budget over the next five years, but are well past the point when they can save money by cancelling whole programmes; those went years ago. Instead, they pore over spreadsheets, looking for a £2,000 saving here, a £3,000 saving there, which means the effort to make the budget balance consumes a huge amount of their time, and services are gradually degraded. This is particularly stark in education, where new technologies are introduced all the time and schools have to spend money to keep up.

And it’s striking in healthcare too. The Powys health board, which is funded separately but faces the same kind of challenges, ended the last financial year having overspent by £33m. In response, it has proposed to close most of the county’s eight community hospitals, reducing inpatient beds from about 146 to as few as 60.

after newsletter promotion

Austerity is not just about the loss of big headline services. It is also about small indignities that add up to a lot: fewer roads get gritted in winter, which makes getting around harder; services are being concentrated in a smaller number of towns, making them harder to access. And all of this is being made worse by the county’s demographics. The more rural a place is, the older its population and the faster its average age is increasing. Powys exemplifies that trend, which creates ever more demand for the council’s services and ever less money to pay for them.

For years, the amount of money Powys council has spent looking after people has been creeping ever closer to what it spends educating children. In 2023-34, the sums reached level. The next year, social care took the lead, and in 2025-26, that gap grew. Over that period, for every £100 the council spent, the school budget has remained constant at £34, but the social care budget has increased from £35, to £37, to £39. As that share creeps remorselessly upwards, something else has to give. This is the grim reality that councillors face.

S ean Davies’s family has farmed in Merthyr Cynog, at the head of the Ysgir valley north of Brecon, for five generations. His kids were educated – alongside his neighbours’ children – at a small school in the village of Cradoc. But in autumn 2020, just as a new spike in Covid cases was causing the government in Cardiff to start reimposing lockdowns in towns in the south Wales valleys, he and his wife, Becky, heard that the school was to close.

“Bang! That suddenly came out of nowhere, didn’t it?” said Davies. “They refused anything like a public meeting because everything was closed. Even then, when things started getting back to some sort of normality, a consultation landed on us with no public meetings of any kind. They pay no real attention to the consultation. I mean, it’s a laugh, a paper exercise. You ask if they’re conniving or just crap? Really, it’s a bit of both.”

Country people are used to being patronised, and parents are often therefore reluctant to praise the nature of a rural education, not least because they’re aware of all the city facilities that they lack, as well as the inconvenience of having to drive their kids everywhere. However, there is a real value to a slower-paced education, where children learn things later, discover things for themselves, and do so in smaller groups, and that’s true from Orkney to Cumbria to Cornwall to Powys.

“You know yourself, rural kids, they’re different,” Davies said to me. “It’s just, it’s a different education, and I get the feeling sometimes people roll their eyes when you try to make a case for rural education, because it’s as if they’re automatically thinking that you’re trying to say that it’s better. But I’ve never ever said that. Just said it’s different.”

After they got the bad news, the Davieses and their neighbours mobilised, found political allies, pushed back in every way they could, but month by month, other parents took their kids out of Cradoc and the school dwindled. By the time their son was the last boy in his class, their daughter’s friends were leaving and the council voted to close the school in March 2022, they realised they had to give up. Every morning, the Davies kids are now driven half an hour to a different village school, which is – for now – still open. Every morning, they pass the abandoned buildings where they once studied.

“I don’t think people appreciate the damage it’ll do to the community. I find it very hard,” said Davies. “And cutting things doesn’t automatically mean an improvement. It’s the same like rugby players now leave Wales to go and play in England. They’re doing really well there, but they’re gone. That’s exactly what will happen in Powys. People will just look around and unless they’re involved in farming or tourism, which is under pressure as well, they won’t stay.”

This is what people in Gladestry are concerned about. It’s quite normal for locals to leave and work in England or in Cardiff in their 20s, then return to Powys once they have children of their own. But it becomes much harder to draw them back, let alone to attract other young families, if there is nowhere nearby to educate their children.

This is bad for the economy because without young adults, businesses struggle to attract employees, as do key services. When Powys county council tried to hire specialised staff in 2022 to support primary schools, it was unable to find any suitable candidates. But it’s also just bad for a community; a village needs people of all ages.

O ne morning in early October, a dozen or so Gladestry residents drove to Llandrindod Wells – a crumbling ex-spa town of 6,000 people that’s now better known for the periodic arrests of county lines drugs gangs than for people taking the waters – to stand outside the brick-and-glass county council offices.

The council had much on its agenda that morning, but the protesters were interested in only one item – No 15. Councillors were due to vote on whether to change the rules so that a school could be closed only with the approval of the full council, rather than just the cabinet, in a motion proposed by Gladestry’s local councillor.

These lobbying efforts were slightly shambolic, since no one knew what most councillors looked like. That meant they regularly engaged people in conversation about “item 15” only to discover their target was an ordinary council employee trying to get into the office in time for a video call. But the few councillors who did stop and chat seemed to be on side.

Item 15 did indeed pass – full council approval would be needed to close schools – but something potentially even more significant for the school’s fate emerged. The council was forced to extend its consultation period because it had left out of its original document the fact that, although the closure would save the council £43,000 in the first year, changes to the funding formula meant it would actually cost the council money thereafter. The omission reset the clock on the consultation period, which will now end in December, rather than October, pushing the whole timetable back by a couple of months.

It looks unlikely, therefore, that there will be enough time to complete the process to close the school before council elections are held in May. If this year’s Senedd voting pattern is repeated, the current Liberal Democrat-Labour coalition will lose control of the council and be replaced by either Reform UK or Plaid Cymru. Both have committed to protecting rural schools, which is great news for Gladestry, but whoever is in charge will find themselves squeezed by the same mathematics.

The council’s plan for escaping this trap involves building “all-through schools” that combine primary and secondary education on a smaller number of single sites. The conundrum is that the council needs to invest in new facilities to do this, but can’t afford to, so it’s stuck in the same doom loop of cuts year after year after year.

The obvious answer to that conundrum, according to most people in Powys, is that they should get more money from outside. Parts of Scotland with equivalently sparse populations to Powys receive more than 50% more funding per head of population as mid-Wales, whereas Powys’ funding is almost exactly at the Welsh average.
